domains.name: Data Commentary & Visuals
domains.summary: Data commentary is where numerical and visual evidence becomes argument: learners must read visuals accurately, select what matters, and write or speak about it with claims calibrated to the evidence rather than exhaustive description. The domain runs from visual literacy (visual types, reading graphs and tables, recognising misleading displays) through the lexicogrammar of trends, proportions and diagrams, to the genre of data commentary and the conventions for labelling, referring to and creating visuals. IELTS Writing Task 1 is treated as a contrast case: it rewards selective description of key features, whereas university data commentary also interprets, explains, compares and qualifies.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to read graphs, tables and diagrams accurately, describe what they show in precise language, and use them as evidence in your own writing, including creating clear and honest visuals of your own.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Reading common graph and table types and describing trends, proportions and processes precisely, using visuals from subject modules such as business, science and engineering.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Moving from test-style description to data commentary that locates, highlights, interprets and qualifies, typically in an extended project or report.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific visual conventions in lab, project and business reports, including captions, in-text references and creating charts from learners’ own data.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Commenting on results in dissertations with appropriately hedged interpretation, and critically evaluating visuals in sources.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Data commentary in results and discussion chapters and articles, figures designed to journal requirements, and visual argument in research presentations.

domains.name: Digital Scholarship Tools
domains.summary: Academic work is mediated by digital tools (learning platforms, word processors, reference managers, shared documents, machine translation and automated writing evaluation) whose effective and ethical use is rarely taught explicitly. This domain treats these tools as part of academic literacy practices rather than as separate technical skills (Lea & Jones, 2011), emphasising critical and transparent use: tools support but do not replace learners’ judgement, their outputs must be checked, and their permitted use is set by institutional policy. Because products change quickly, topics are framed around transferable functions and decisions rather than named applications.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to use the digital tools of university study, including learning platforms, word processing, reference managers, shared documents, translation and feedback tools, efficiently, critically and within your institution’s rules.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Orientation to the learning platform, file management and word processing, with transparent and critical use of machine translation.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Institutional systems and policies, reference managers, machine translation and automated feedback as supports, and digital collaboration in project work.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Efficient assignment workflows: styles, reference managers, shared documents and critical use of feedback tools.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Managing dissertation-scale work: versioning, reference libraries, collaboration and supervisor feedback in shared documents.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Thesis-scale document management, research data and file organisation, and a professional online presence.

domains.name: Multimodal Composition
domains.summary: Academic communication increasingly combines writing with images, layout, colour, sound and movement, and university assessment now includes posters, infographics, podcasts, video essays and e-portfolios. This domain treats multimodal composition as meaning-making with distinct semiotic resources (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006), addresses the design of key academic multimodal genres (MacIntosh-Murray, 2007), and treats accessibility as a design requirement from the outset rather than an afterthought (World Wide Web Consortium, 2023). Academic expectations of argument, evidence and attribution carry over into these genres, even though the means of realising them change.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how images, layout and text work together, and how to design posters, infographics and digital assignments that are clear, persuasive and accessible to all your readers.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Awareness of how layout and images make meaning, developed through simple posters and short digital tasks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Posters and short recorded or digital presentations as assessed work, with attention to text economy and reading paths.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific multimodal assessments (posters, video essays, e-portfolios) and accessible document design.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Research posters, infographics for professional audiences and accessible dissertation formatting.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Conference posters, visual abstracts and public-engagement graphics, and accessibility in theses and publications.

domains.name: Academic Numeracy Language
domains.summary: Academic numeracy language is the lexicogrammar and conceptual precision needed to talk and write about quantities, measurements, statistics and mathematical relations in English. Errors here are rarely ‘just language’: confusing per cent with percentage points, using ‘significant’ loosely or misplacing a unit changes the claim. The domain runs from accurate number expressions and approximation, through units and mathematical expression, to statistical vocabulary and consumer-level interpretation of statistical claims, drawing on research into statistical literacy (Gal, 2002) and risk communication (Gigerenzer et al., 2007). EAP teachers without statistical training may wish to co-teach the later topics with subject or mathematics-support colleagues.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to talk and write about numbers, measurements and statistics precisely, and to understand what the statistical claims in your reading do and do not show.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Number expressions, units and basic statistical terms in subject modules such as mathematics, science and business, in both speech and writing.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Precision and approximation in data commentary, relative versus absolute change, and the everyday versus statistical senses of key terms.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific notation and units, statistical vocabulary in methods and results, and reading statistical claims in sources.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Consumer-level interpretation of p-values, confidence intervals and effect sizes in research reading and dissertations.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Accurate statistical and mathematical expression in theses and articles, following field and journal conventions.

topics.name: Types of visuals and their functions
topics.description: Recognise the main visual forms in academic texts (line graphs, bar charts, pie charts, scatterplots, tables, flowcharts, diagrams, maps and photographs) and the relationship each is designed to show: change over time, comparison between categories, part–whole composition, distribution, association between variables, sequence or spatial layout. Knowing what a visual is for guides how it is read and which language is needed to describe it.
masteryEvidence: Names common visual types and matches each to the relationship it typically represents (trend, comparison, composition, distribution, association, process, location)
Explains why a given dataset is better shown as a table than a graph, or as a line graph than a pie chart
Identifies visuals whose type is mismatched to their data, such as a line joining unordered categories or a pie chart of non-exclusive responses
Distinguishes data displays (graphs, tables) from conceptual visuals (models, flowcharts, photographs) and predicts the different commentary each invites
topics.assessmentPrompt: Describe four small datasets in words (monthly temperatures over two years; market share of five firms; height and weight of 40 students; twelve exact values a reader must look up) and ask which visual suits each and why. Check that choices follow the relationship in the data (time → line graph; part–whole → pie or stacked bar; association → scatterplot; look-up → table) and are justified by function rather than appearance.

topics.name: Reading graphs and charts
topics.description: Read graphs and charts systematically: check the title, axes, scales, units, legend and source before interpreting; then extract values, compare across series, and identify the overall pattern, exceptions and notable features. Accurate reading at the levels of individual data, relationships between data and inferences beyond the data underpins both data commentary and critical evaluation of others’ visuals.
masteryEvidence: Checks title, axis labels, units, scale intervals and legend before interpreting any values
Reads specific values accurately, including from logarithmic, dual or non-zero-based axes
Identifies the overall pattern and the most important exceptions, peaks, crossovers or outliers
Distinguishes what the graph shows directly from inferences or predictions beyond the plotted data
Notes missing information that limits interpretation, such as absent units, sample size or source
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a two-series line graph whose y-axis starts at 40 and whose final point is marked as an estimate. Ask one read-off question, one comparison between the series and one ‘what might explain this / what would you expect next’ question. Check read-off accuracy, correct units in the comparison, whether the learner notices the truncated axis and the estimate, and whether the inference is marked as tentative.

topics.name: Reading tables
topics.description: Navigate tables by identifying what rows and columns represent, the units, totals, notes, abbreviations and significance markers; locate specific values; and compare across rows or columns to identify the main pattern. Research articles often carry findings in tables that the prose mentions only briefly, so efficient table reading is essential for accurate source use.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the variables in rows and columns, the units and any totals or subtotals
Uses table notes, footnote symbols and abbreviations (n, M, SD, asterisks for significance) to interpret entries
Locates specific values quickly and compares across rows and columns accurately
States the most important pattern or difference in a table and points to the cells that show it
Checks claims in the prose against the table and notices discrepancies or overstatement
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a results table from a research article (means, standard deviations, sample sizes and a significance asterisk) together with the article’s one-sentence summary of it. Ask the learner to find two specific values, state the main pattern and judge whether the summary sentence represents the table accurately. Check correct use of the notes and whether any overstatement in the summary is noticed.

topics.name: Describing trends and change
topics.description: Describe change over time precisely using verbs (rise, fall, fluctuate, level off, peak), nouns (an increase in, a decline of), degree and speed modifiers (slightly, sharply, a gradual rise), prepositions of quantity and time (from … to, by, at, over the period) and appropriate tense. Precise trend language lets writers summarise patterns economically and select only the changes that matter to their point.
masteryEvidence: Uses verb and noun patterns for change with accurate prepositions (rose by five points to 20%; an increase of 5% in output)
Chooses degree and speed modifiers proportionate to the size of the change and the scale of the graph, rather than defaulting to dramatic intensifiers
Selects tense appropriately: past for completed periods, present for what the figure shows, modal or future forms for projections
States an overall trend before detail and groups similar changes
Varies structures (verb, nominal, there was) without loss of precision
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a line graph with three series over ten years, including one small change, one sharp change and one plateau. Ask for a 100-word description. Check preposition accuracy (by/to/from/of/in), whether modifiers are proportionate (a two-point change is not ‘dramatic’), whether an overall trend precedes detail, and tense consistency.

topics.name: Describing proportions and comparisons
topics.description: Express proportions and comparisons in data precisely, using fractions, percentages, ratios and multiples (a third of, 42% of, a ratio of 3:1, twice as many as), quantifiers (the majority, a substantial minority, nearly all) and comparative and superlative structures with numbers. This allows exact, checkable comparisons between groups and categories rather than vague impressions.
masteryEvidence: Expresses proportions with accurate articles, prepositions and agreement (a third of respondents were; the proportion of graduates was)
Uses comparative and multiplicative structures with numbers accurately (twice as likely as; 15 percentage points higher than; the largest share)
Matches quantifiers (most, the majority, a substantial minority) to the actual proportions they describe
Chooses between percentage, fraction and ratio according to which makes the comparison clearest for the reader
Avoids or clarifies ambiguous multiplicative comparisons such as three times more than
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a pie chart and a grouped bar chart of survey responses from two groups. Ask for five sentences comparing the groups. Check agreement after proportion/percentage/fraction phrases, comparative grammar with numbers, whether quantifiers fit the values (is 52% ‘the vast majority’?) and whether at least one sentence compares between groups rather than within one.

topics.name: Data commentary
topics.description: Write commentary that uses data as evidence: locate the visual and summarise what it shows, highlight the findings that matter for the writer’s purpose, and interpret them by explaining, comparing with expectations or previous studies, acknowledging limitations and drawing implications whose strength matches the evidence. Data commentary is the core of results and discussion writing across disciplines and differs from description-only tasks such as IELTS Writing Task 1.
masteryEvidence: Opens with a location statement or summary that links the visual to the purpose of the text
Selects and highlights the two or three findings that matter for the argument rather than describing everything
Offers explanations or implications and calibrates their strength with hedges, approximators and qualifications
Distinguishes association from causation and acknowledges alternative explanations or data limitations
Organises commentary from general to specific and relates it to research questions, expectations or prior studies
Explains how a commentary differs from a test-style description of the same visual
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a figure plus a one-line research question and ask for a 150-word commentary. Check for a location or summary statement; selection of findings relevant to the question; at least one interpretive move (explanation, comparison with expectation or literature, implication); appropriate hedging, with no causal claim drawn from correlational data; and the absence of exhaustive description.

topics.name: Describing processes, diagrams and maps
topics.description: Verbalise non-numerical visuals: the stages, branches and loops of processes and cycles in flowcharts; the components and spatial relations in diagrams of structures and systems; and spatial change shown in maps and plans. This draws on sequencing language, voice choice, purpose and result expressions and locative prepositions, and supports explaining scientific, technical and planning visuals in reports, examinations and presentations.
masteryEvidence: Describes a process or cycle in logical order, including decision branches and loops (if … otherwise; the cycle then repeats)
Chooses passive or active voice according to whether the process or the agent is in focus
Describes spatial relations and changes on maps or plans accurately (to the north of, adjacent to, was replaced by, was extended)
Opens with an overview of the whole process or layout before detail
Groups stages into phases rather than enumerating each step mechanically
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a flowchart with one decision branch and one loop (for example a manuscript review process). Ask for a 120-word description. Check that the overview states the start, end and number of main phases, that the branch and loop are expressed accurately, and that voice choices follow focus.

topics.name: Figure and table captions
topics.description: Number, title and caption figures and tables according to the required style, write informative titles and notes that let the visual stand alone, define abbreviations, symbols and units, and acknowledge the source of reproduced or adapted visuals. Correct labelling makes visuals referable in the text and, when visuals or data come from others, is part of academic integrity.
masteryEvidence: Numbers tables and figures in separate sequences in order of first mention
Writes concise, informative titles that state what is shown, for whom or where, and when
Adds notes defining abbreviations, symbols and units so the visual can be understood without the main text
Attributes reproduced or adapted visuals and data using the required wording (e.g., Adapted from; Data from) with a matching reference-list entry
Follows the placement and formatting conventions of the required style guide or journal
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a figure adapted from a published source with a vague title (‘Graph 1’) and undefined abbreviations. Ask the learner to rewrite the number, title, notes and attribution in the course style. Check numbering, informativeness of the title, definition of abbreviations, attribution wording and a matching reference-list entry.

topics.name: Creating effective visuals
topics.description: Choose the visual form that best serves a message and audience, and design it for clarity and honesty: an appropriate chart type, honest scales and baselines, minimal non-data decoration, direct labelling, accessible colour and enough context (units, sample size, uncertainty). Well-designed visuals let readers check claims quickly and are increasingly assessed in reports, posters and theses.
masteryEvidence: Selects a chart type that matches the relationship to be shown and the audience, and justifies the choice
Sets scales, baselines and aspect ratios that represent the data without exaggerating or concealing differences
Removes non-essential decoration (3D effects, heavy gridlines, redundant legends) and labels data directly where possible
Uses colour purposefully and accessibly, without relying on colour alone to distinguish series
Includes units, sample sizes and, where relevant, indicators of uncertainty such as error bars or confidence intervals
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a cluttered spreadsheet-default chart (e.g., a 3D pie chart or a bar chart with a distant legend) and its data. Ask them to redesign it for a stated message and audience and annotate three changes. Check that each change is justified by the message, honesty or accessibility (type, scale, labelling, colour) rather than by appearance alone.

topics.name: Recognising misleading visuals
topics.description: Recognise design and data choices that distort a visual’s message (truncated or inconsistent axes, selective time windows, dual axes, area and 3D distortion, mismatched chart types, missing denominators or uncertainty) and judge whether conclusions drawn from the visual are justified. This is a component of statistical literacy and of the critical evaluation of sources.
masteryEvidence: Identifies truncated, inconsistent or dual axes and explains how they change perceived magnitude
Detects selective time windows and omitted comparison groups
Recognises area, volume and 3D effects that misrepresent proportions
Asks for missing context (denominators, sample size, uncertainty, data source) before accepting a visual claim
Distinguishes deliberate or careless distortion from defensible conventions, such as a non-zero baseline on a line graph of small variations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show two versions of the same data (one with a truncated y-axis and a narrow time window, one complete) with a headline claim. Ask whether the headline is justified. Check that the learner names the specific design choices, explains their effect, asks about the data source or denominator, and does not dismiss every non-zero baseline as dishonest.

topics.name: Referring to visuals in text
topics.description: Integrate visuals into prose by referring to them explicitly and purposefully (Figure 2 shows; as shown in Table 1; see Figure 3), placing references where the reader needs them, choosing verbs that suit visual subjects and the strength of the claim (show, indicate, illustrate, suggest), and telling the reader what to notice. This links visual evidence to the argument instead of leaving visuals to speak for themselves.
masteryEvidence: Refers to every visual in the text by number, at or before the point where it appears
Uses a range of integration structures (visual as subject, as-clauses, parenthetical references) grammatically, avoiding blends such as as Figure 2 shows that
Chooses verbs with visual subjects that match the claim (shows vs suggests vs illustrates)
Tells the reader what to notice rather than merely pointing to the visual
Avoids duplicating in the text every value already shown in the visual
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph in which three figures are referred to poorly (no number, ‘the following graph’, a reference after the visual, ‘as Table 1 shows that’). Ask the learner to revise it. Check for numbered references, grammatical as-clauses, a statement of what to notice, and removal of duplicated values.

topics.name: Virtual learning environments
topics.description: Navigate the institution’s virtual learning environment and related systems to find module information, assessment briefs, readings, recordings, announcements and feedback; submit work correctly through submission portals; and keep track of deadlines and notifications. Missed instructions, unread feedback and failed submissions are avoidable sources of difficulty, especially in a first term.
masteryEvidence: Locates module handbooks, assessment briefs, marking criteria, reading lists and recordings for a given module
Submits assignments correctly, checking file format, file name and the submission receipt
Retrieves and opens returned feedback, including inline comments and audio or video feedback
Manages notifications and announcements so that key information is not missed
Uses discussion areas and messaging within the platform in line with module expectations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Set a 15-minute task on the learner’s actual platform: find the assessment brief, criteria, deadline, submission point and most recent recording for one module, and locate the feedback on a previous submission. Check speed and accuracy, and whether the learner checks the submission receipt and opens the feedback comments rather than looking only at the grade.

topics.name: Reference management software
topics.description: Use reference management software to collect, organise and annotate sources, insert in-text citations and generate reference lists in a required style, and check the output for errors. Reference managers save time and reduce inconsistency, but they reproduce whatever metadata they are given, so users still need to know what a correct reference looks like.
masteryEvidence: Imports references from databases, DOIs and PDFs and corrects incomplete or inaccurate metadata
Organises a library with folders, tags and notes that reflect a project’s themes
Inserts citations and generates a reference list in a specified style through a word-processor plug-in
Checks generated citations and references against the style guide and corrects common errors (capitalisation, missing pages, wrong item type, duplicates)
Backs up and, where relevant, shares a library with collaborators
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five sources (a journal article with a DOI, a book chapter, a report, a web page and a dataset) and ask the learner to import them, insert citations into a short paragraph and generate a reference list in the course style. Check metadata accuracy, item types and style compliance, and whether the learner finds and corrects at least two automatic errors.

topics.name: Academic word processing
topics.description: Use the word-processing functions that support academic documents: paragraph and heading styles, automatic numbering, generated contents pages, captions and cross-references, section breaks, headers, footers and page numbers, templates, and comments. Structure-based formatting saves time in long documents, keeps formatting consistent and makes documents accessible and easier to revise.
masteryEvidence: Applies heading styles and generates an automatic table of contents
Inserts captions for tables and figures and cross-references that update automatically
Uses section breaks to manage different page numbering or orientation
Applies a required template or formatting specification (margins, spacing, font) efficiently
Navigates a long document using the navigation pane and styles
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an unformatted ten-page document with manually formatted headings, typed figure numbers and a typed contents list. Ask the learner to restructure it with styles, numbered captions, cross-references and a generated contents page within 30 minutes. Check that headings appear in the navigation pane, the contents page updates, and cross-references update when a figure is moved.

topics.name: Translation tools in reading and drafting
topics.description: Use machine translation (MT) strategically and transparently: to support comprehension of difficult texts, to check understanding, to explore wording and, where permitted, to support drafting, while recognising MT’s characteristic errors (terminology, register, lost hedging, ambiguity), verifying its output and complying with assessment rules. MT is a legitimate plurilingual resource, but undeclared or wholesale use in assessed writing can breach integrity policies and bypass language development.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes permitted from prohibited uses of MT in a given assessment according to institutional and module policy
Uses MT to support comprehension while checking key terms against discipline glossaries or dictionaries
Identifies typical MT errors in academic text (mistranslated technical terms, lost or added hedging, register shifts, fluent but inaccurate output)
Post-edits MT output critically and explains the changes made
Declares MT use where required and keeps a record of how it was used
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an academic paragraph machine-translated into English from a language the learner reads, containing three seeded errors (a mistranslated technical term, a lost hedge and a register shift). Ask the learner to identify and correct the problems and to say whether this use would be permitted under a given module policy. Check error detection, especially of the lost hedge, and accurate interpretation of the policy.

topics.name: Digital collaboration tools
topics.description: Use shared documents, comments, suggestion and track-changes modes, version history and cloud workspaces to co-author and review academic work: setting permissions, giving and responding to comments constructively and concisely, resolving suggestions, and keeping a clear record of contributions. Digital collaboration is now the default medium for group projects and for much supervisor feedback.
masteryEvidence: Sets up a shared document or workspace with appropriate permissions and a clear structure
Uses suggestion or track-changes mode and comments rather than silently overwriting others’ text
Writes comments that are specific, actionable and appropriately mitigated
Accepts, rejects or replies to suggestions and comments, and resolves threads
Uses version history to recover text and to evidence individual contributions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a shared draft with five comments from a supervisor or peer, some of them ambiguous. Ask the learner to respond to each (accept, reject with a reason, or ask for clarification) using comments and suggestions. Check use of the appropriate functions, the clarity and politeness of replies, and that no text is silently overwritten.

topics.name: File and version management
topics.description: Organise, name, version and back up academic files systematically: consistent folder structures and file names, clear distinction between working and submitted versions, local and off-device backups, and secure storage of sensitive material. Good file management prevents lost work and confusion between drafts and, for research students, is the basis of research data management.
masteryEvidence: Uses a consistent folder structure and file-naming convention (e.g., date, module, version)
Distinguishes working drafts from submitted versions and retrieves any earlier version on request
Maintains at least two backups, one of them off-device, and has tested recovery
Stores sensitive or personal data securely in line with institutional policy
Documents research files and data so that another person could understand and locate them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show where the latest and the submitted versions of their last assignment are, and to explain how they would recover the work if their laptop failed. Check naming consistency, version clarity and the existence of an off-device backup; for research students, check whether research data are stored according to policy.

topics.name: Digital etiquette and online presence
topics.description: Communicate appropriately in digital academic spaces (forums, group chats, video calls, social media and professional networks), adapting tone, formality and response expectations to channel and audience, and manage an academic online presence and privacy (profiles, researcher identifiers, what to share publicly). Digital interactions persist and are searchable, so pragmatic misjudgements can have lasting effects.
masteryEvidence: Adapts formality, length and tone to the channel and relationship (course forum, group chat, professional network)
Follows participation norms in video calls (camera, microphone, chat, turn-taking)
Creates and maintains an accurate, professional academic profile appropriate to their stage, such as an institutional profile or researcher identifier
Makes informed decisions about privacy and about what personal or research information to share publicly
Recognises online conflict or inappropriate content and responds through appropriate channels
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three scenarios: a group-chat message to a peer who has missed a deadline; a forum reply disagreeing with a classmate; a public post about one’s own research. Ask the learner to draft each. Check register shifts across channels, mitigation in disagreement, and awareness of public visibility and confidentiality.

topics.name: Automated writing evaluation tools
topics.description: Use automated writing evaluation (AWE) tools, including grammar and style checkers, automated feedback platforms and AI-based feedback features, as one input among others: interpret their suggestions critically, accept or reject them on principled grounds, recognise what they cannot judge (argument, content, disciplinary appropriateness) and comply with rules on permitted use. Uncritical acceptance can introduce errors, flatten voice and, where rewriting features are used, breach assessment rules.
masteryEvidence: Explains which kinds of issue AWE tools detect reliably and which they miss or misjudge
Accepts or rejects suggestions with reasons based on grammatical knowledge or disciplinary convention
Identifies false alarms (e.g., flagged technical terms or necessary passives) and missed problems
Combines AWE feedback with teacher and peer feedback in a revision plan
Checks whether a tool’s features, especially rewriting or paraphrasing functions, are permitted for a given assessment
topics.assessmentPrompt: Run one of the learner’s paragraphs through an AWE tool and ask them to work through ten suggestions, accepting or rejecting each with a reason. Check the accuracy of their decisions, especially rejection of inappropriate suggestions (such as replacing a technical term or removing a necessary passive), and whether they notice problems the tool missed.

topics.name: Multimodal literacy
topics.description: Understand how image, layout, colour, typography and text combine to make meaning, and analyse how a multimodal text directs attention through salience, reading path, framing and the placement of information. This awareness underpins both critical reading of academic multimodal texts and the design of posters, slides and digital assignments.
masteryEvidence: Describes how layout, salience and framing guide a reader’s path through a poster, slide or web page
Explains the division of labour between image and text in an academic visual, stating what each conveys that the other does not
Uses a basic metalanguage of visual design (salience, framing, reading path, information value) to analyse examples
Identifies disciplinary conventions in visual communication, such as the visual types typical of conference talks in their field
Critiques a multimodal text for coherence between its modes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show a research poster or infographic for 30 seconds, then hide it. Ask what the learner noticed first, second and third. Show it again and ask which design features (size, position, colour, framing) produced that order. Check for use of design concepts beyond ‘it looks nice’ and for recognition of how image and text share the message.

topics.name: Designing academic posters
topics.description: Design an academic poster that communicates a clear main message at a glance and supports conversation in a poster session: a hierarchy of title, key finding and supporting sections; a logical reading path; economical text; visuals that carry the evidence; and legibility at viewing distance. The poster is a genre with its own norms, not a shrunken paper.
masteryEvidence: States the poster’s main message in a headline or prominently placed key finding
Organises sections along a clear reading path using columns, numbering or visual flow
Reduces text to essential claims within a word budget, using phrases and lists where appropriate
Uses visuals as the primary evidence, each with an informative caption
Ensures legibility (type size, contrast) and accessible design at the intended viewing distance
Explains design decisions in relation to the audience and the session format
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a text-heavy draft poster (around 1,200 words in abstract-style paragraphs). Ask them to identify three problems and propose a redesign plan with a word budget and a headline finding. Check that they prioritise the main message, cut text, convert prose results into visuals where possible, and attend to reading path and legibility.

topics.name: Infographics and visual summaries
topics.description: Condense information into visual summaries (infographics, visual abstracts and one-page summaries) for academic and public audiences: select the essential message, structure it visually, and preserve accuracy, attribution and appropriate qualification. Visual summaries are increasingly used in assessment and research dissemination, and they risk oversimplification when impact is pursued at the expense of accuracy.
masteryEvidence: Selects one core message and a small number of supporting points for the summary
Structures content with a clear visual hierarchy and reading path
Preserves the accuracy and essential qualifications of claims when simplifying
Represents numbers honestly and in formats suited to the audience
Attributes data and images and includes the source reference
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a research abstract and ask the learner to sketch, in 20 minutes, a visual abstract or infographic for a public audience. Check that the core finding is accurate and appropriately qualified, the structure is clear, numbers are represented honestly and in an accessible format, and the source is cited.

topics.name: Video essays and digital assessments
topics.description: Produce assessed multimodal genres (podcasts, video essays, narrated presentations, e-portfolios and websites), understanding their purposes, criteria and conventions, and orchestrating speech, text, image and sound to build an academic argument with appropriate attribution of sources and media. These genres keep the core academic expectations of argument, evidence and citation while changing the means of expression.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the purpose, audience and assessment criteria of a digital assignment, including the academic expectations that still apply
Plans with a script or storyboard showing how the modes are coordinated to build an argument
Integrates and attributes sources, images, music and footage in ways suited to the medium
Uses a spoken register and pacing suited to recorded academic delivery
Provides accessibility features such as captions or transcripts where required
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a brief for a five-minute video essay and ask the learner to storyboard the first minute with script excerpts and source attributions. Check that the argument is explicit, the modes complement rather than duplicate one another, sources and media are attributed, and captions or a transcript are planned.

topics.name: Accessible academic documents
topics.description: Produce documents, slides and media that are accessible to readers with disabilities and to assistive technologies: structured headings created with styles, meaningful alternative text for images and charts, sufficient colour contrast, meaning not conveyed by colour alone, descriptive link text, readable typography, and captions or transcripts for audio-visual content. Accessibility is an institutional and often legal expectation, and it improves clarity for all readers.
masteryEvidence: Applies heading styles and a logical reading order rather than relying on visual formatting
Writes alternative text that conveys the purpose and key message of an image or chart, and provides a longer description for complex visuals
Checks colour contrast and avoids relying on colour alone to convey meaning
Uses descriptive link text and table structures that assistive technologies can interpret
Provides captions or transcripts for recorded audio-visual work
Runs an accessibility checker and interprets its results critically, recognising what it cannot judge
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short document containing a chart, a decorative image, colour-coded text and ‘click here’ links. Ask the learner to make it accessible and explain each change. Check heading structure, quality of alternative text (key message rather than ‘graph of data’), handling of the decorative image, colour-independent meaning and descriptive links.

topics.name: Expressing quantities accurately
topics.description: Express numbers, fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios and rates accurately in prose, together with the grammar around them: articles and of-phrases (a third of, two-thirds of the sample), agreement (a quarter of respondents were), per cent versus percentage, number of versus amount of, rates (per capita, per 1,000) and multiplicative forms. Accurate quantity expressions are the basis of every claim made from data.
masteryEvidence: Reads aloud and writes fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios and large numbers correctly in words and figures
Uses partitive and quantity structures with accurate articles, prepositions and agreement
Distinguishes per cent (with a number) from percentage (a proportion), and number of from amount of
Expresses rates and ratios unambiguously (per 1,000 population; a ratio of 3:2; one in five)
Converts between equivalent forms (0.25, 25%, a quarter, one in four) to suit the reader
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present ten quantities in mixed forms (0.05, 3/8, 1:4, 12.5%, 2.3 million, 4 per 1,000) and ask the learner to use each in a full sentence about a sample. Check partitive structures and agreement, the per cent/percentage distinction, and the expression of decimals and large numbers.

topics.name: Approximation and precision
topics.description: Approximate and round quantities appropriately (approximately, roughly, just under, well over, in the region of, nearly a third, an estimated) and decide when exact figures or approximation better serve the reader and purpose. Approximators also function as hedges: they signal the writer’s commitment to exactness and must be consistent with the figures and with the precision of the measurement.
masteryEvidence: Uses approximators and boundary expressions accurately (just under, just over, nearly, slightly more than, in excess of)
Rounds figures to a precision consistent with the measurement and sample (e.g., not reporting 33.33% for three cases)
Chooses between exact and approximate expression according to audience and genre (results section vs lay summary)
Keeps approximate verbal expressions consistent with the figures cited alongside them
Avoids both false precision and unnecessary vagueness
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a small table of exact values and ask for two short summaries: one for a results section and one for a lay summary. Check that the results version gives appropriately rounded figures, the lay version uses approximators accurately (‘just under half’ for 47%, not for 41%), and neither introduces false precision.

topics.name: Basic statistical vocabulary
topics.description: Understand and use core statistical terms accurately in reading and writing: population and sample, variable, mean, median, mode, range, standard deviation, distribution, correlation, outlier, significance, error and bias. Several of these words have everyday meanings that differ from their technical sense (significant, normal, error, random, confidence, bias), so precise use is essential for credible methods and results writing.
masteryEvidence: Defines core descriptive and inferential terms accurately in plain English
Distinguishes everyday from statistical senses of significant, random, error, bias, normal and confidence
Uses the terms with conventional collocation and grammar (a strong positive correlation between X and Y; statistically significant at the .05 level; normally distributed)
Chooses between mean and median when summarising skewed data and explains the choice
Recognises common symbols and abbreviations (M, SD, n, N, r, p, CI) in texts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five sentences mixing everyday and statistical senses (e.g., ‘There was a significant number of complaints’; ‘The difference was significant, p = .03’). Ask the learner to label each sense and rewrite any ambiguous sentence for a quantitative report. Check that statistical significance is distinguished from importance and that ‘significant’ is not used without a test.

topics.name: Interpreting statistical claims
topics.description: Read and interpret inferential statistics at an informed consumer level: understand what p-values, confidence intervals and effect sizes do and do not indicate, distinguish statistical significance from practical importance, and recognise how sample size and design limit conclusions. This allows learners to evaluate quantitative sources and report them accurately without overstating them.
masteryEvidence: Explains in plain English what a p-value does and does not indicate, avoiding the reading that it is the probability that a hypothesis is true
Distinguishes statistical significance from the size and practical importance of an effect
Interprets a confidence interval as a range of values compatible with the data and comments on its width
Recognises when a non-significant result is misreported as evidence of no effect
Reports a quantitative finding from a source with appropriate hedging, effect-size information and reference to design
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an abstract reporting ‘a significant effect (p = .04)’ from a large sample with a small effect size, together with a news headline calling it ‘a major breakthrough’. Ask the learner to judge the headline and rewrite it. Check whether they separate significance from size, mention sample size or design, and avoid both overclaiming and dismissing the finding.

topics.name: Relative and absolute change
topics.description: Distinguish relative from absolute change (per cent versus percentage points; relative versus absolute risk; rates versus counts) and choose and interpret framings that do not mislead. The same result can be presented as ‘a 50% reduction’ or as ‘a fall from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000’, and readers and writers need to recognise how framing shapes judgement.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes a change in percentage points from a percentage change and calculates both from the same data
Converts a relative risk reduction into an absolute risk reduction when given a baseline
Identifies sources that report only relative figures and explains why this may mislead
Chooses transparent framings (absolute figures, natural frequencies) when writing for non-specialist readers
Distinguishes counts from rates and notices missing denominators
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present ‘Unemployment rose from 4% to 5%’ and ask the learner to express the change in percentage points and as a percentage change, and to say which a newspaper might choose and why. Then give ‘a treatment halves the risk of X’ with a baseline of 2 in 1,000 and ask for an absolute statement. Check the calculations and the explanation of framing effects.

topics.name: Units and measurement
topics.description: Report measurements using SI units and symbols correctly (symbols versus names, a space between number and unit, prefixes, no plural or full stop on symbols, compound units such as m/s or kg m⁻³) and follow discipline and style-guide conventions where these differ. Correct use of units is a precondition for credibility and replicability in science, engineering and health writing.
masteryEvidence: Writes unit symbols and prefixes with correct case (mg, kHz, μm, mL or ml) and without plural or full-stop forms (not kgs or cm.)
Separates number and unit symbol with a space, following any style-guide exceptions consistently
Expresses compound units in one consistent format
Says measurements aloud in a form consistent with the written symbol (‘five milligrams per litre’)
Keeps units and their formatting consistent across text, tables and figures
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short methods paragraph containing eight unit errors (e.g., 5Kg, 20 mins., 3 mls, inconsistent 37°C and 37 °C, m/s/s). Ask the learner to correct it with reference to an SI summary and the course style guide. Check symbol case, spacing, plurals, compound units and internal consistency.

topics.name: Language of mathematical expression
topics.description: Read and write mathematical expressions in academic prose: verbalising equations and inequalities, introducing and defining variables (where x denotes; let n be), integrating displayed equations into sentences with appropriate punctuation, and using conventional phrasing for relationships (is proportional to, tends to, is a function of). This is needed wherever formulae carry the argument, as in science, engineering, economics and quantitative social science.
masteryEvidence: Reads equations, inequalities and common notation aloud accurately, including grouping (the square of x plus y vs x plus y, all squared)
Defines every variable and parameter on first use, typically with a where-clause
Integrates displayed equations into sentences grammatically, with appropriate punctuation
Uses conventional verbal formulations for relationships (is directly proportional to, increases linearly with, is inversely related to)
Distinguishes italic quantity symbols from upright unit symbols and function names
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a displayed formula from the learner’s discipline (e.g., a regression equation or a kinematic formula). Ask the learner to read it aloud and to write the sentence that introduces it and defines its terms. Check accuracy of verbalisation including grouping, a where-clause defining all variables, punctuation around the display, and conventional relational verbs.

dependencies.reason: Reading a graph presupposes recognising its type and the relationship it encodes, which determines where to look for the pattern
Reading scale values, percentages and large or decimal numbers off axes draws on secure control of number expressions
Knowing that tables serve exact look-up and multi-variable comparison sets an appropriate purpose for reading them
Locating specific values in rows and columns applies scanning for numbers and terms
Interpreting cell values, decimals, percentages and rates requires secure number expressions
The pattern, magnitudes and turning points must be extracted accurately from the graph before they can be described
Trend description requires principled choice between past simple for completed periods and present simple for what a figure shows
Proportion statements are built from fractions, percentages and ratios expressed accurately in prose
Comparing proportions relies on comparative and multiplicative structures (twice as many as, higher than, the largest)
Describing flowcharts and cycles applies the sequencing, voice and purpose language of process description to a visual source
Describing structural diagrams, plans and maps draws on part–whole and spatial description
Recognising how flowcharts, cycles and maps encode sequence and space guides how they are verbalised
An informative title presupposes knowing what kind of relationship the visual is designed to show
Attributing reproduced or adapted visuals depends on understanding that others’ data and images require citation
In-text references depend on a consistent numbering and labelling scheme for tables and figures
Experience of moving between prose and visuals as a reader shows writers where references are needed and what they should direct attention to
Verbs used with visuals as subjects (show, indicate, illustrate, demonstrate) differ in strength and complementation
Commentary on change over time requires precise, proportionate trend language
Highlighting statements frequently compare groups and proportions, which requires accurate comparison language
Data commentary typically opens with a location statement that refers the reader to the visual
Highlighting statements and interpretations must be calibrated to what the data can support
Interpretive commentary must avoid inferring causation from association and must consider alternative explanations
Detecting distortion requires reading axes, scales and encodings accurately in the first place
Treating visuals as constructed and open to question extends the stance of critical reading to non-verbal evidence
Designing honest visuals requires knowing which scale, area and selection choices distort
Choices of chart type, detail and labelling depend on what the intended reader needs and the purpose of the text
Navigating the platform depends on understanding the institutional vocabulary it is organised around (module, assessment brief, submission, extension)
Checking and correcting generated references requires knowing the elements and format of a correct reference-list entry
Importing records directly from catalogues and databases presupposes being able to search and export from them
Citations are inserted and reference lists generated through the word processor, so basic document handling is needed first
Using MT well presupposes seeing one’s other languages as legitimate resources for learning rather than something to hide or avoid
Verifying MT output for key terms relies on effective use of learner, bilingual and specialist dictionaries
Judging when MT-produced wording can be submitted as one’s own work depends on understanding plagiarism and authorship
Comments, suggestion mode and track changes are document features that build on basic word-processing control
Shared workspaces require consistent naming, folder structure and versioning to avoid conflicting copies
Agreeing who edits what, and how, is a prerequisite for using shared documents without conflict
Choosing tone and mitigation in digital messages applies face and politeness considerations to new channels
Accepting or rejecting flagged issues is more reliable when learners know their own recurrent error patterns
Familiarity with common academic visual forms supplies the concrete examples from which broader multimodal analysis develops
Understanding mode as a dimension of register prepares learners to treat image and layout as meaning-making choices
Poster design applies salience, reading path and image–text relations to a specific genre
Posters rely on figures that carry the evidence, so honest and legible chart design is needed
Text economy on posters depends on removing redundancy and compressing claims
Infographics depend on composing visual hierarchy and image–text relations deliberately
Visual summaries of data require honest, audience-appropriate representation of numbers
Most infographics address non-specialist readers and draw on plain-language and lay-summary principles
Video essays and podcasts require orchestrating speech, image, text and sound as complementary resources
Recording, screen-sharing and delivering speech to a camera or microphone are component skills of most digital assessments
Digital assignments must attribute audio-visual sources, images and music, which uses conventions for diverse source types
Accessible structure (headings, reading order, captions) is created through styles and automatic features rather than manual formatting
Recognising how colour, layout and images carry meaning shows what must be conveyed in alternative forms
Quantity expressions build on quantifiers and determiners (a number of, much/many, fewer/less, each)
Fractions, percentages and the number of / a number of all raise agreement choices that presuppose general agreement control
Approximators modify quantity expressions, which must already be accurate
Boundary approximations (just over half, nearly twice as many) combine approximators with comparative structures
Terms such as mean, range and standard deviation are defined and used through quantity expressions
Several statistical terms (significant, normal, error, bias) are sub-technical words whose specialised sense must be separated from everyday use
Interpreting p-values, confidence intervals and effect sizes presupposes knowing what the terms and symbols denote
Judging what a statistical result licenses depends on understanding what designs support causal claims
Effect sizes and risk statistics are often reported in relative terms, so interpreting them draws on the relative–absolute distinction
The percentage-point versus percentage-change distinction is expressed through, and confused in, proportion and comparison language
Relative and absolute framings are most often met in statements of change over time
Measurements combine a numerical value with a unit, so number expression must be secure
Unit names, prefixes and quantity names are part of discipline terminology learned and used consistently
Verbalising formulae builds on reading numbers, fractions, powers and operations aloud and in prose
Introducing variables and parameters is a form of operational definition

guidance.summary: Graph comprehension research shows that format shapes interpretation: viewers tend to read line graphs as continuous trends and bar charts as discrete comparisons, and novices often lack the graph schemas experts use to extract the main message (Shah & Hoeffner, 2002). Teaching visual types functionally, by the relationship each encodes, rather than as a vocabulary list gives learners a schema for both reading and choosing visuals. Disciplinary variation matters: Rowley-Jolivet’s (2002) analysis of conference visuals shows marked differences between fields in their reliance on graphical, numerical and figurative images.

activities.title: Same data, different displays
learnerActions: Examine one small dataset (e.g., enrolments by faculty over three years) shown as a table, a grouped bar chart, a line graph and a pie chart
For each display, write the one message a reader would notice first
Decide which display best serves each of three stated purposes (showing change, comparing faculties in one year, showing share of the total)
Justify each choice in two sentences using functional language (shows change over time; compares categories)
activities.intendedInsight: The same numbers foreground different relationships depending on the visual form, so choosing a visual is an argumentative decision.
activities.rationale: Shah and Hoeffner (2002) review evidence that display format influences which features viewers extract; contrasting formats for identical data makes this effect visible to learners.

activities.title: Visual audit of a disciplinary source
learnerActions: Collect all the visuals from a textbook chapter or article in their own field
Classify each by type and by the relationship it shows
Compare classifications with a peer from a different discipline
Note which types are frequent, rare or absent in each field and suggest why
activities.intendedInsight: Fields favour different visual repertoires, so knowledge of visual types must partly be built from one’s own discipline’s texts.
activities.rationale: Rowley-Jolivet (2002) found disciplinary differences in the kinds of visuals used in conference papers; a learner-led audit applies that insight to texts learners will actually read.

difficulties.pattern: “Any chart will do — I just pick the one that looks best.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Pie charts with many slices or for non-part–whole data, 3D charts, and line graphs joining unordered categories in learners’ own reports.
difficulties.response: Return to the relationship–type mapping and ask learners to state the message before choosing the form; redesign one of their charts with them. Do not present a rigid one-data-type-one-chart rule, since several forms are often defensible.

difficulties.pattern: Treating tables as not really ‘visuals’ and skipping them when reading.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries of articles that omit key findings reported only in tables; tables absent from learners’ own reports where they would be the clearest form.
difficulties.response: Teach tables explicitly as the preferred display for exact look-up and small datasets (Tufte, 2001), and set tasks whose answer is available only in a table.

diagnostic.task: Show three visuals from different disciplines (a scatterplot, a flowchart and a stacked bar chart) and ask what kind of relationship each shows and what question a reader could answer from it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names each type, identifies association, sequence and composition-with-comparison respectively, and poses questions about relationships rather than single values.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names the types correctly but describes content only as individual values or labels.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Mislabels types (e.g., calls the scatterplot a line graph) or cannot say what relationship is displayed.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation, concentrate on the five or six most common types in subject textbooks, linked to subject content. On pre-sessional courses, connect types to the language each requires (trends, proportions, processes). In UG in-sessional work, move to discipline-specific forms (box plots, forest plots, Gantt charts, schematics) using learners’ own module materials.

guidance.summary: Friel, Curcio and Bright (2001) distinguish reading the data (extracting values), reading between the data (comparing and finding relationships) and reading beyond the data (extrapolating and inferring); EAP learners often stop at the first level. Shah and Hoeffner (2002) show that comprehension depends on display features, graph-reading skill and content knowledge, and that novices attend to individual points rather than global patterns. A consistent frame–pattern–exception routine, practised on graphs from learners’ own disciplines, addresses both problems.

activities.title: Frame, pattern, exception
learnerActions: Before looking at the data, read and paraphrase the title, axes, units and legend aloud to a partner
State the single overall pattern in one sentence
Identify two exceptions or notable points (peaks, troughs, crossovers, outliers)
Write one question the graph cannot answer
activities.intendedInsight: Graph reading is staged: skipping the frame causes most misreadings, and the pattern matters more than any single value.
activities.rationale: The routine targets the global-pattern reading that Shah and Hoeffner (2002) identify as weak in novices and moves learners through the levels described by Friel et al. (2001).

activities.title: Three-level question writing
learnerActions: In pairs, take a graph from a subject textbook
Write three questions, one at each level: read the data, read between the data, read beyond the data
Swap questions with another pair and answer them
Discuss which questions were hardest and what knowledge they required
activities.intendedInsight: Inference beyond the data relies on content knowledge and should be signalled as tentative.
activities.rationale: Learner-generated questions make Friel et al.’s (2001) levels operational and reveal where subject knowledge, rather than the graph, is doing the work.

difficulties.pattern: “I can read the numbers, but I don’t see the point.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Descriptions that list values point by point without any overall statement.
difficulties.response: Require an overview sentence before any detail and model how experts summarise. Do not respond by supplying more trend vocabulary: the gap is selection, not lexis.

difficulties.pattern: Misreading scales, units or legends, such as treating thousands as units or attributing values to the wrong series.
difficulties.revealedBy: Order-of-magnitude errors; values assigned to the wrong series; units omitted in comparisons.
difficulties.response: Make a frame check (title, axes, units, legend) a habit using a short checklist, and deliberately include non-standard scales (logarithmic, truncated, dual axes).

difficulties.pattern: Assuming that the graph shows a cause.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements such as ‘the graph shows that advertising caused sales to rise’.
difficulties.response: Separate ‘what the graph shows’ from ‘what might explain it’ in two columns, and return to this distinction when teaching data commentary.

diagnostic.task: Give an unfamiliar bar chart from another discipline and, after 60 seconds, ask for a two- or three-sentence spoken summary.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Frames the chart (what is measured, units, groups), states the main pattern and one exception, and marks any explanation as speculation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reads accurate values and identifies a pattern but omits the frame, or presents an explanation as fact.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists values without a pattern, or misreads the scale or legend.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners may need explicit work on scales and units alongside subject mathematics. Pre-sessional courses can integrate graph reading with reading research texts. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, focus on discipline-specific forms (error bars, box plots, forest plots) and on reading beyond the data cautiously.

guidance.summary: Tables are the default display for exact values and small datasets (Tufte, 2001) and are pervasive in research articles, yet EAP reading instruction often neglects them. Friel et al.’s (2001) levels of comprehension apply here too: learners must move from locating values to comparing and interpreting patterns. Swales and Feak (2012) treat tables as a central source for data commentary, which presupposes that they can be read accurately and efficiently.

activities.title: Table anatomy and notes hunt
learnerActions: Label the parts of a research table: number and title, row labels, column headings, body and notes
Find and explain every symbol and abbreviation using the table notes
Answer five look-up questions within a time limit
Explain to a partner one cell whose meaning depends on a note
activities.intendedInsight: Headings and notes carry meaning that is essential for interpreting the values.
activities.rationale: Making the table’s structure explicit secures the ‘reading the data’ level before higher-level interpretation (Friel et al., 2001).

activities.title: Text versus table check
learnerActions: Read a results paragraph and the table it refers to
Highlight each claim in the paragraph and find the supporting cells
Mark each claim as accurate, selective or overstated
Rewrite one overstated claim so that it matches the table
activities.intendedInsight: Writers select from and interpret tables; readers should verify rather than rely on the prose.
activities.rationale: Prepares for data commentary, in which writers highlight selectively from tables (Swales & Feak, 2012), and builds a habit of checking.

difficulties.pattern: Reading every cell from top left to bottom right.
difficulties.revealedBy: Slow, linear reading; inability to state the main pattern; time overruns in reading tasks.
difficulties.response: Teach purposeful entry: read the title, headings and notes first, then scan for the comparison the question requires. Avoid timed drills until the structure is understood.

difficulties.pattern: Ignoring notes and abbreviations.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misinterpreting asterisks, confusing n with a percentage, or treating a standard deviation as a second mean.
difficulties.response: Require learners to gloss every symbol before interpreting, and connect the glosses to work on statistical vocabulary.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a four-by-five table to a peer in under one minute without reading out every number.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains what the rows and columns show, names the main comparison and supports it with two key values, using the notes correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives accurate values but no clear main comparison, or overlooks the notes.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot explain what the rows and columns represent, or misreads values.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: simple frequency and percentage tables from subject textbooks. Pre-sessional: tables in short research articles and in learners’ own project data. UG and PGT in-sessional: complex results tables with statistical notation, where table reading connects with interpreting statistics.
reviewNotes: Empirical research specifically on L2 learners’ table reading is limited; this guidance extrapolates from graph comprehension research.

guidance.summary: Trend language is heavily rehearsed for IELTS Writing Task 1, so many learners arrive with a large repertoire of change verbs but less control of prepositions, proportionate modifiers and selection. Instruction should prioritise accuracy of pattern (rose by vs rose to; an increase in vs an increase of) and proportionality over lexical variety, and should present trend description as a component of commentary rather than an end in itself (Swales & Feak, 2012). Corpus consultation can show which modifier–verb combinations are typical in academic prose; Boulton and Cobb’s (2017) meta-analysis suggests that corpus use is generally beneficial for learning, with effects varying by context.

activities.title: Proportionate modifiers
learnerActions: Place modifiers (slightly, moderately, considerably, sharply, dramatically) on a scale of magnitude
Match them to changes on graphs with clearly labelled scales
Rewrite a description that uses ‘dramatically’ for every change
Justify each choice by reference to the size of the change and the axis scale
activities.intendedInsight: Degree words make factual claims about magnitude and must be warranted by the data.
activities.rationale: Treats modifiers as calibrated claims rather than stylistic variety, consistent with Swales and Feak’s (2012) emphasis on accuracy and strength of claim in commentary.

activities.title: Corpus check of change patterns
learnerActions: Search an academic corpus for increase and decrease as nouns and as verbs
Classify the prepositions that follow (in, of, by, to, from) and what each signals
Compare these patterns with sentences in their own drafts
Correct two of their own sentences and explain the change
activities.intendedInsight: Prepositions after change words carry precise meanings: an increase in names what changed; an increase of names how much.
activities.rationale: Corpus-based noticing of form–meaning patterns; Boulton and Cobb (2017) report generally positive effects of corpus use on lexicogrammatical learning.

difficulties.pattern: “The more different verbs I use, the better my description.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of rare synonyms (soared, plummeted, skyrocketed) for modest changes; elegant variation that obscures whether changes are comparable.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge the test-preparation origin of this habit, then show expert data commentary in which a small set of verbs recurs and precision comes from figures and modifiers. Do not ban vivid verbs; ask whether the data warrant them.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing by, to, of and in after change words.
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘Sales increased to 5%’ when an increase of five points was meant; ‘an increase of sales’.
difficulties.response: Use contrast pairs with numerical consequences (rose by five points to 25% vs rose to 5%) and ask learners to work out the starting value each sentence implies.

difficulties.pattern: Describing every fluctuation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long point-by-point descriptions with no overview or grouping.
difficulties.response: Impose a tight word limit and require an overview sentence followed by grouped changes.

diagnostic.task: Give six trend sentences about a graph, containing preposition, tense and proportionality errors, and ask the learner to correct them with reference to the graph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Corrects all preposition and tense errors and flags disproportionate modifiers by referring to the graph’s values.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Corrects grammatical errors but accepts disproportionate modifiers.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not detect by/to confusion or tense errors.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from explicit contrast with IELTS Task 1 habits, and those still preparing for a test can be shown which features transfer. In UG in-sessional work, embed trend description in lab reports, economics and geography assignments, where it is a brief step towards explanation.
reviewNotes: The characterisation of IELTS-preparation habits rests on practitioner observation; Green (2007) is relevant background on washback but does not analyse Task 1 language specifically.

guidance.summary: Comparing proportions combines grammatical systems that are individually familiar but error-prone in combination: quantifiers, partitive of-phrases, subject–verb agreement and comparative structures with numbers (Biber et al., 1999; Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999). Precision is a matter of judgement as well as grammar, because quantifiers such as ‘most’ or ‘a large proportion’ make claims that readers will check against the figures. Teaching should pair each pattern with its numerical consequences and connect comparisons to the point being argued (Swales & Feak, 2012).

activities.title: Quantifier calibration
learnerActions: Individually place quantifier phrases (nearly all, the vast majority, most, over half, a substantial minority, few) on a 0–100% line
Compare placements in groups and discuss overlaps and disagreements
Check against example sentences from published articles supplied by the teacher
Rewrite three sentences from their own drafts so that quantifiers and figures agree
activities.intendedInsight: Quantifiers have fuzzy but bounded ranges; giving the figure alongside the quantifier removes ambiguity.
activities.rationale: Making learners’ implicit ranges explicit exposes disagreement between readers and motivates pairing words with numbers.

activities.title: Comparison grammar with consequences
learnerActions: Read pairs such as ‘Group A was three times as likely as Group B’ and ‘Group A was three percentage points more likely’
Calculate what each sentence implies, given a base rate
Write comparisons for a dataset using a multiple, a difference and a ratio
Check a partner’s sentences against the numbers
activities.intendedInsight: Comparative structures with numbers encode different arithmetic relationships.
activities.rationale: Links comparative grammar (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999) to the numerical precision later needed for relative and absolute change.

difficulties.pattern: Agreement after proportion phrases (‘the percentage of students are’; ‘a third of the participants was’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Agreement errors with partitives and with proportion, percentage and number as head nouns.
difficulties.response: Teach the contrast between a head noun such as percentage or proportion (singular verb) and a partitive with a plural complement (30% of students are). Note acceptable variation rather than over-correcting notional agreement.

difficulties.pattern: Using ‘three times more than’ ambiguously.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comparisons that could mean three or four times as many, or that do not match the figures.
difficulties.response: Prefer ‘three times as many as’ or give both values; ask learners to compute what their sentence claims.

difficulties.pattern: Using ‘the majority’, ‘most’ or ‘a significant number’ loosely.
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘The vast majority’ for 55%; ‘a significant number’ with no statistical test.
difficulties.response: Pair every quantifier with its value and reserve ‘significant’ for its statistical sense in quantitative reports.

diagnostic.task: Give a table of four groups’ percentages and ask for two comparison sentences, one using a multiple and one using a difference.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Both sentences are grammatical, arithmetically correct and clearly framed (as many as; percentage points higher than).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Grammar is mostly accurate but the multiple or difference is miscalculated or ambiguous.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Comparative structure and agreement are faulty and the comparison is unclear.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: survey and market data in business and social science modules. Pre-sessional: comparisons within short data commentaries and project reports. UG in-sessional: discipline-specific comparisons (shares, ratios, odds) where precision is assessed.

guidance.summary: Swales and Feak (2012) describe data commentary as the writer’s purposeful use of data, such as highlighting results, assessing theories or expectations, comparing and evaluating, organised through location elements, highlighting statements with appropriate qualification, and discussion of implications or problems. Move analyses of results and discussion sections (Yang & Allison, 2003; Basturkmen, 2009) show that commenting on results, by explaining them, comparing them with the literature and evaluating them, is where much of the argument is made. Teaching should therefore contrast description with commentary explicitly and practise strength-of-claim decisions; Hyland’s (1998) work on hedging shows that appropriate claim strength is a disciplinary judgement, not a stylistic preference.

activities.title: From description to commentary
learnerActions: Compare a test-style description and an expert commentary of similar figures (teacher-written or published)
Label the moves in each: location, overview, highlighting, explanation, qualification, implication
Identify what the expert text omits and what it adds
Rewrite their own description as commentary for a given research question
activities.intendedInsight: Commentary is selective and driven by purpose; description is exhaustive and neutral.
activities.rationale: Rhetorical consciousness-raising through move labelling follows Swales and Feak’s (2012) approach and makes explicit a contrast that learners from test-preparation backgrounds may not have met.

activities.title: Strength-of-claim continuum
learnerActions: Order interpretations of a single result from strongest to weakest (proves, shows, indicates, suggests, may reflect)
Decide which is warranted, given information about sample size, design and effect size
Rewrite over-claiming sentences from sample student texts
Add one alternative explanation to their own commentary
activities.intendedInsight: Interpretive claims must be calibrated to the design and the evidence.
activities.rationale: Hedging in results and discussion sections signals the writer’s assessment of the evidence (Hyland, 1998); practising calibration on a single result isolates that judgement.

difficulties.pattern: “Commentary means describing every number accurately.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Long descriptions with no interpretation or link to purpose, often mirroring a Task 1 overview-plus-details structure.
difficulties.response: Make the purpose explicit by giving a research question and asking which findings matter for it; set word limits that make exhaustive description impossible.

difficulties.pattern: Claiming causation from association.
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘The data prove that X causes Y’ drawn from cross-sectional or observational data.
difficulties.response: Ask what design produced the data; model language of association (is associated with, coincides with, is consistent with) and offer alternative explanations.

difficulties.pattern: Hedging so heavily that no claim remains.
difficulties.revealedBy: Stacked hedges (‘it might possibly suggest that this could perhaps’).
difficulties.response: Show that commentary must commit to an interpretation and that one well-placed hedge usually suffices. Do not respond by banning hedges.

diagnostic.task: Give a short student commentary on a bar chart and ask the learner to evaluate it as commentary rather than as language.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies that it describes without highlighting or interpreting, notes any over-claiming, and proposes specific additions (location, highlighting, explanation, qualification).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices that it is mainly description but suggests only general improvements.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Evaluates it only for grammatical or lexical accuracy.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: short commentaries on project data, contrasted explicitly with IELTS Task 1.
