UG in-sessional: lab and project reports where commentary is brief and shaped by discipline. PGT: dissertation results and discussion chapters that compare findings with the literature. PGR: results and discussion chapters and articles, where commentary carries the contribution and field norms of claim strength are critical.
reviewNotes: Moore and Morton (2005) compare IELTS Writing Task 2 with university writing; the Task 1 contrast drawn here extends their general finding of test–university divergence rather than reporting a Task 1 study.

guidance.summary: Describing processes and structures is a long-recognised rhetorical function in scientific and technical English (Trimble, 1985), and Swales and Feak (2012) treat process description as a building block of graduate writing. Diagrams add a translation problem: learners must turn spatial and visual relations (arrows, branches, loops, layout) into linear prose. Teaching should focus on overview-first organisation, voice chosen according to focus (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999), and accurate expression of branching and cycles, using diagrams from learners’ disciplines rather than only test-style process diagrams.

activities.title: Diagram to text and back
learnerActions: Pair A describes a flowchart in writing
Pair B, without seeing the original, draws the diagram from the description
Compare the drawn and original diagrams and locate ambiguities (a missing branch, unclear order)
Pair A revises the description
activities.intendedInsight: A good description lets a reader reconstruct the visual; ambiguities show up as drawing errors.
activities.rationale: Information-gap reconstruction gives authentic feedback on clarity and treats description as verbal–visual translation, a relationship Trimble (1985) emphasises in scientific and technical discourse.

activities.title: Voice and focus decisions
learnerActions: Mark each stage in a process description as agent-focused or process-focused
Choose active or passive voice for each stage and justify the choice
Compare with an expert description from a discipline textbook
Discuss where the passive is conventional and where it is a choice
activities.intendedInsight: Voice in process description follows focus and convention, not a rule that the passive is objective.
activities.rationale: Grounds voice choice in information focus (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999) and counters the myth that the passive is inherently more objective.

difficulties.pattern: Using first, second, then, next for every stage.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mechanical enumeration with no grouping into phases and loops or branches ignored.
difficulties.response: Teach grouping (the process consists of three main phases) and connective alternatives (once, after which, at this point). Avoid giving learners long lists of sequencers to memorise.

difficulties.pattern: Map and plan descriptions that list features without orientation or change.
difficulties.revealedBy: No compass or relative directions; no explicit before–after contrast.
difficulties.response: Have learners complete a before–after comparison grid first, then write from it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain orally, in about 60 seconds, a three-stage cycle diagram from their field.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives an overview, follows the correct sequence including the return to the start, and uses appropriate voice and purpose or result links.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Follows the correct sequence but gives no overview or relies on mechanical sequencing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Confuses the sequence or omits key stages.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: science and engineering process diagrams, and test-style maps for learners still preparing for a test. Pre-sessional: process description within method and explanation sections. UG in-sessional: discipline diagrams (system architectures, life cycles, supply chains) in reports and presentations.

guidance.summary: Style guides such as the APA Publication Manual (American Psychological Association, 2020) specify numbering, titles, notes and attribution for tables and figures, but conventions vary across styles, disciplines and journals, so learners need a principle as well as a format: a visual should be interpretable on its own and its provenance traceable. Tufte (2001) treats clear, thorough labelling as part of graphical integrity. Attribution of reproduced and adapted visuals is an under-taught area of source use that connects directly with citation and integrity teaching.

activities.title: Stand-alone test
learnerActions: Exchange figures, without the surrounding text, with a peer
Write down what the peer’s figure shows and any questions it leaves unanswered
Return the questions to the author
Revise titles and notes until a reader can interpret the figure without the text
activities.intendedInsight: Titles and notes must carry enough information for a visual to be understood in isolation.
activities.rationale: Operationalises Tufte’s (2001) principle of clear, detailed labelling through reader feedback.

activities.title: Style comparison
learnerActions: Compare table and figure conventions in two style guides or two journals in their field
Tabulate differences (placement, capitalisation, order of notes, attribution wording)
Reformat one figure from one style to the other
Write a one-line rule for their current assignment
activities.intendedInsight: Formats differ, but the principles of numbering, informativeness and attribution are shared.
activities.rationale: Builds transferable knowledge rather than dependence on a single format, with the APA manual (2020) as a worked reference point.

difficulties.pattern: “If I drew the chart myself from someone else’s data, I don’t need to cite it.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Charts redrawn from reports or articles with no source line or reference.
difficulties.response: Explain that both data and design are attributable; teach wording such as ‘Data from’ and ‘Adapted from’ and link it to the institution’s citation policy.

difficulties.pattern: Titles that name the chart type rather than the content (‘Bar chart’, ‘Table 1’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Uninformative titles that do not say what is measured, for whom or when.
difficulties.response: Offer a heuristic (what – who or where – when) and check with the stand-alone test.

diagnostic.task: Present three captions of varying quality for the same figure and ask the learner to rank them and explain the ranking.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Ranks by informativeness, completeness of notes and correctness of attribution, citing specific omissions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices formatting differences but not problems with notes or attribution.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Ranks by length or appearance.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: basic numbering, titles and attribution in reports. UG and PGT in-sessional: compliance with the required style in lab reports and dissertations. PGR: journal-specific figure requirements and, for theses and articles, permission to reproduce published figures.
reviewNotes: Copyright permission for reproducing figures in deposited theses varies by jurisdiction and repository policy; this topic addresses attribution only.

guidance.summary: Tufte’s (2001) principles of graphical integrity and economy of non-data ink are a useful starting point, though some of his more austere prescriptions are debated and are best presented as heuristics. Shah and Hoeffner (2002) show that design choices predictably shape what viewers notice, so the designer should decide the message first and then choose the form. Accessibility requirements, such as not relying on colour alone and ensuring sufficient contrast (World Wide Web Consortium, 2023), are part of good design rather than an afterthought.

activities.title: Redesign clinic
learnerActions: Bring a chart from their own coursework or a spreadsheet default
State in one sentence the message it should convey
Redesign it by applying three principles (type matched to relationship, honest scale, direct labelling)
Show before and after versions to peers, who say what message each conveys
activities.intendedInsight: Design changes alter what readers perceive, so the message should drive the design.
activities.rationale: Applies evidence that display features shape interpretation (Shah & Hoeffner, 2002) to learners’ own visuals.

activities.title: Integrity and accessibility checklist
learnerActions: Co-construct a checklist from graphical integrity principles and accessibility requirements
Apply it to three published figures from their field
View their own chart in greyscale or with a colour-vision simulator
Revise any element that fails the checklist
activities.intendedInsight: Honesty and accessibility are design requirements, not finishing touches.
activities.rationale: Combines graphical integrity (Tufte, 2001) with accessibility criteria (World Wide Web Consortium, 2023) in a routine learners can reuse.

difficulties.pattern: “The software’s default settings must be right.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Unmodified defaults: 3D effects, legends far from the data, automatically truncated axes, arbitrary colours.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to inspect and override defaults. Do not assume that confidence with software implies design judgement.

difficulties.pattern: “More visual effects make it look professional.”
difficulties.revealedBy: 3D bars, shadows, gradients and decorative images that obscure values.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to read exact values from decorated and plain versions of the same chart and compare accuracy and speed.

difficulties.pattern: Varying chart types across a report for the sake of variety.
difficulties.revealedBy: Different chart types for parallel data in successive sections, making comparison harder.
difficulties.response: Explain that consistency aids comparison and that form should change only when the relationship changes.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain three design decisions in a chart they produced for an assignment.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Justifies type, scale and labelling by message and audience, and mentions an accessibility decision.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Justifies the chart type only, or justifies decisions by appearance.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot explain choices beyond the software defaults.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: simple charts in project reports. UG and PGT in-sessional: lab reports, dissertations and posters, with discipline conventions such as error bars in the sciences. PGR: publication-quality figures to journal specifications, including representation of uncertainty and colour accessibility.
reviewNotes: Later visualisation research has questioned whether all decoration (‘chartjunk’) harms comprehension or memorability; Tufte’s prescriptions are presented as heuristics, and no study outside the bibliography is relied on here.

guidance.summary: Tufte’s (2001) ‘lie factor’, the ratio of the size of an effect shown graphically to its size in the data, gives learners a concrete test for distortion. Gal (2002) frames the critical evaluation of statistical messages, including their graphical presentation, as a core part of adult statistical literacy and proposes ‘worry questions’ about data sources, samples and representations. Instruction should avoid simplistic rules (for example, that every axis must start at zero) and instead teach learners to ask what comparison a design invites and whether the data support it (Shah & Hoeffner, 2002).

activities.title: Lie factor workshop
learnerActions: Measure the visual change (bar length, area) and the data change in three media graphics
Calculate an approximate ratio for each
Redraw one graphic honestly
Write a one-sentence verdict on whether its headline is supported
activities.intendedInsight: Distortion can be quantified, and perceived magnitude depends on design.
activities.rationale: Tufte’s (2001) lie factor turns graphical integrity into a measurable check.

activities.title: Worry questions on real graphics
learnerActions: Bring a chart from news, policy or social media relevant to their field
Apply a short list of critical questions (source, sample, denominator, time window, scale, uncertainty)
Rate the visual’s trustworthiness and note what further information would change the rating
Present the case to the class
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluating a visual means questioning the data behind it, not only its design.
activities.rationale: Adapts Gal’s (2002) worry questions for statistical literacy to visual evidence.

difficulties.pattern: “Any graph that doesn’t start at zero is lying.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Rejecting conventional line graphs of temperatures, exchange rates or test scores.
difficulties.response: Distinguish bar charts, where length encodes value and the baseline matters, from line graphs, where position encodes change; ask what comparison the design invites.

difficulties.pattern: “Graphs in published sources are objective.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncritical reuse in essays of visuals from advocacy or commercial reports.
difficulties.response: Connect to source evaluation: ask who produced the visual, for what purpose and from what data.

diagnostic.task: Show a 3D pie chart in which a front slice looks largest although it is not, and ask what the chart shows.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notices the perspective distortion, checks the labels and states the actual ranking.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives the correct ranking from the labels but cannot explain the distortion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reads the ranking from apparent visual size alone.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: media and policy graphics used as sources in essays. UG in-sessional: critical evaluation of visuals in sources and in learners’ own work. PGT: visuals in research and grey literature used in dissertations, overlapping with methods critique.

guidance.summary: Swales and Feak (2012) identify location elements, sentences or clauses that point the reader to a table or figure, as a characteristic opening of data commentary, and highlight the grammatical traps of as-clauses. Yang and Allison (2003) describe a preparatory move in results sections that orients readers to visuals. Trimble (1985) treats visual–verbal relationships as a rhetorical feature of scientific and technical writing. Teaching should address both the grammar of reference and the rhetorical decision about what the reader should notice.

activities.title: As-clause clinic
learnerActions: Sort sentences into correct and incorrect as-clauses (As shown in Table 1, …; As can be seen from Figure 2, …; *As Figure 1 shows that …)
Formulate the pattern from the examples
Correct five faulty sentences
Find three examples in an article from their discipline and check them against the pattern
activities.intendedInsight: As-clauses follow a small number of fixed patterns; blending them produces common errors.
activities.rationale: Targets a grammatical problem that Swales and Feak (2012) highlight in location statements.

activities.title: What should the reader notice?
learnerActions: Highlight every reference to a visual in a results section
Classify each as pointing only or pointing and guiding
Rewrite pointing-only references so that they guide the reader to a finding
Discuss when a bare parenthetical reference is enough
activities.intendedInsight: Effective references direct attention to the finding that matters.
activities.rationale: Draws on move analysis of results sections (Yang & Allison, 2003) to show that references to visuals serve the argument.

difficulties.pattern: Blending structures (‘As Table 1 shows that …’; ‘As shown in Figure 2 shows …’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Ungrammatical location statements, especially with as-clauses.
difficulties.response: Teach two or three core patterns explicitly before offering alternatives, and link verb choice to complementation.

difficulties.pattern: “The figure speaks for itself.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Figures inserted with no reference or only a bare ‘(see Figure 1)’.
difficulties.response: Ask a peer to read the text cold and report what they think the figure is for; discuss the mismatch.

difficulties.pattern: Repeating every value from the visual in the text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that duplicate table contents.
difficulties.response: Teach a division of labour: the visual holds the detail, the text says what it means.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write two sentences introducing a figure into a report.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces a grammatical, numbered reference and a clear statement of the key point.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Produces a correct reference without guidance, or guidance with an as-clause error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives no numbered reference or an ungrammatical structure.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: simple numbered references in reports. Pre-sessional and UG in-sessional: integrating visuals in project and lab reports. PGT and PGR: managing many visuals across chapters, cross-referencing and journal conventions.
reviewNotes: Trimble (1985) is cited for the general principle of visual–verbal relationships in scientific and technical English; chapter location should be checked.

guidance.summary: Lea and Jones (2011) show that students’ digital practices in higher education are embedded in disciplinary and institutional literacy practices rather than being separable technical skills. Platform use is largely institution-specific, so instruction should use the real system, early, with authentic tasks. Feedback deserves particular attention: returned comments are often embedded in platform tools and may go unread, and Carless and Boud (2018) stress that feedback has value only when students engage with it and act on it.

activities.title: Platform treasure hunt
learnerActions: Find the assessment brief, marking criteria, deadline and submission point for one current module
Locate the most recent lecture recording and the reading list
Adjust notification settings so that announcements are seen
Compare routes with a partner and note any information that was hard to find
activities.intendedInsight: Key information is distributed across the platform; systematic navigation prevents missed requirements.
activities.rationale: An authentic task on the real system, early in the course, addresses the institution-specific nature of these practices (Lea & Jones, 2011).

activities.title: Feedback retrieval
learnerActions: Locate the feedback on a previous submission, including inline comments
Summarise the three most important comments in their own words
Plan one specific action for the next assignment
Share the plan with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Feedback is often hidden behind the grade; finding and reading it is the first step in using it.
activities.rationale: Supports the engagement with feedback that Carless and Boud (2018) identify as necessary for uptake.

difficulties.pattern: “I pressed submit, so it’s done.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Wrong file uploaded, no receipt saved, late submission caused by last-minute upload problems.
difficulties.response: Teach a submit–check–save-receipt routine and encourage submitting well before the deadline.

difficulties.pattern: Looking only at the grade.
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback files and inline comments left unopened.
difficulties.response: Build feedback retrieval into class tasks so that opening and summarising feedback becomes routine.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show where they would find the marking criteria and the submission point for an upcoming assignment.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates both quickly and states the deadline and file requirements.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds one of them, or needs prompting.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot locate either.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: orientation in the first week using real tasks. UG and PGT in-sessional: brief refreshers at induction, focusing on feedback retrieval and submission checks.
reviewNotes: This topic is largely institution-specific and has limited language content; it may sit better as an orientation topic in the Academic Culture domain.

guidance.summary: Reference managers automate formatting, but output quality depends on metadata and on the user’s knowledge of the required style (American Psychological Association, 2020). Learners who rely on them without understanding reference structure often submit lists with wrong item types or capitalisation. Emanuel (2013) reports that users value citation management tools but need support to use them well, so library and EAP staff can usefully teach the tool alongside citation conventions. A further reason to import by DOI or database record is verification: AI tools can generate plausible but non-existent references (Walters & Wilder, 2023).

activities.title: Fix the import
learnerActions: Import a set of references, some of which have deliberately poor metadata
Compare the generated references with the style guide
Correct errors in the library record rather than in the document
Regenerate the list and check it again
activities.intendedInsight: Errors originate in metadata and should be fixed at source.
activities.rationale: Builds the checking habit required by style conventions (American Psychological Association, 2020) and reinforces knowledge of reference anatomy.

activities.title: Verify before you cite
learnerActions: Take a list of references suggested by a search tool or AI chatbot
Attempt to import each one by DOI or database search
Classify each as verified, inaccurate in its details, or not found
Discuss what to do with each category
activities.intendedInsight: A reference that cannot be located should not be cited.
activities.rationale: Responds to documented fabrication of bibliographic citations by AI tools (Walters & Wilder, 2023).

difficulties.pattern: “The software formats references correctly, so I don’t need to check.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Titles in capitals, missing page ranges, web pages typed as journal articles.
difficulties.response: Teach a checking routine against the style guide. Do not ban the tools; their consistency is valuable once output is checked.

difficulties.pattern: A disorganised library.
difficulties.revealedBy: Duplicate entries, no folders or tags, notes lost.
difficulties.response: Introduce an organisation routine early, with tags aligned to the themes of the project.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to review an automatically generated reference list containing five errors.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds most errors and explains their causes (metadata, item type, style setting).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds formatting errors but not wrong item types.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts the list as correct.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: introduce once citation basics are secure. UG and PGT in-sessional: dissertation-scale libraries. PGR: large and shared libraries, and switching styles for different journals.
reviewNotes: Emanuel (2013) is a proposed reference; if it is not accepted, the claim about user support needs should be removed.

guidance.summary: Word processing is usually assumed rather than taught, yet weak control of styles and automatic features causes formatting errors and lost time in long documents such as dissertations. Formatting requirements come from style guides (American Psychological Association, 2020) and institutional rules, and thesis-writing guidance (Paltridge & Starfield, 2020) stresses the management of large documents. Short, task-based demonstrations at the point of need, such as the first report or the start of a dissertation, are likely to be more useful than generic IT sessions.

activities.title: Restructure a messy document
learnerActions: Apply heading styles to a manually formatted document
Generate a contents page
Insert numbered captions and cross-references
Move a figure and update all fields to confirm that numbering follows
activities.intendedInsight: Structure-based formatting maintains itself; manual formatting has to be redone.
activities.rationale: A hands-on before-and-after task makes the time saving visible in a way that demonstration alone does not.

activities.title: Template for the dissertation
learnerActions: Obtain the department’s formatting requirements
Build a template with styles, numbering and caption settings
Test it with sample content including a table and a figure
Share the template with peers and compare
activities.intendedInsight: Setting up structure early prevents late-stage formatting crises.
activities.rationale: Supports the long-document management emphasised in thesis-writing guidance (Paltridge & Starfield, 2020).

difficulties.pattern: Formatting manually, line by line.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent fonts and spacing; manual numbering that goes wrong when sections move.
difficulties.response: Demonstrate the time saved by styles on a long document rather than simply instructing learners to use them.

difficulties.pattern: Fear of ‘breaking’ the document.
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoiding unfamiliar features; copying text into new files to escape formatting problems.
difficulties.response: Practise on copies and save versions before major changes, so that mistakes are recoverable.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show how the headings in their current assignment are formatted.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses heading styles throughout, visible in the navigation pane.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses styles inconsistently.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Formats headings manually only.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: styles and page numbering. UG in-sessional: reports with captions and contents pages. PGT and PGR: dissertation and thesis templates, section breaks and cross-referencing at scale.
reviewNotes: Tool-specific instruction is often best delivered with library or IT services; this topic has limited language content.

guidance.summary: Research suggests that MT used as a revision aid after learners have composed their own text can help reduce lexicogrammatical errors and support noticing (Lee, 2020), while EAP practitioners have raised concerns about its use to produce assessed work and its implications for language development and integrity (Groves & Mundt, 2015). Translanguaging perspectives (García & Li Wei, 2014) support treating learners’ languages as resources rather than interference. Institutional policies vary and are changing quickly as MT and generative AI converge, so teaching should normalise MT as part of a plurilingual repertoire while building critical post-editing and transparent declaration.

activities.title: Compose, translate, compare
learnerActions: Write a short paragraph directly in English
Write the same content in another language they use and machine-translate it into English
Compare the two English versions for terminology, hedging and register
Decide which choices to adopt in a revision and justify each
activities.intendedInsight: MT output is a draft to compare against, not an answer to adopt.
activities.rationale: Mirrors the compose–translate–compare–revise sequence in which Lee (2020) found MT supported revision.

activities.title: Policy scenarios
learnerActions: Read a set of short scenarios describing MT use
Classify each as permitted, permitted with declaration, or not permitted under a given policy
Discuss borderline cases and what information would settle them
Draft a declaration statement for a permitted use
activities.intendedInsight: MT use is governed by context-specific rules, and transparency is the key safeguard.
activities.rationale: Responds to the integrity and pedagogical concerns raised by Groves and Mundt (2015).

difficulties.pattern: “The output is fluent, so it must be right.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Unchecked terminology errors; hedges lost or added in translation.
difficulties.response: Use seeded-error exercises and require key terms to be checked in specialist glossaries.

difficulties.pattern: “Any MT use is cheating, so I have to hide it.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Secretive use, anxiety, or blanket avoidance even where use is permitted.
difficulties.response: Clarify the policy and frame MT as one resource in a plurilingual repertoire, used openly where permitted.

difficulties.pattern: Composing whole texts in another language and translating them.
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner's own account of their process; terminology or hedging that shifts in ways typical of MT output. Differences between in-class and submitted writing are expected and are not evidence on their own.
difficulties.response: Discuss when planning in another language helps and when whole-text translation undermines development and may breach policy. Do not prohibit use of other languages in planning.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they would use MT to read a difficult article and then write a summary of it, under a policy that allows MT for comprehension only.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses MT for comprehension with term checking, writes the summary independently, and notes any declaration required.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes appropriate use for reading but is unclear about the boundary for writing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would translate a summary from another language without checking the policy.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: explicit discussion of policy and critical use for reading. UG and PGT in-sessional: terminology checking and declaration practices. PGR: translation of non-English sources and the ethics of MT in writing for publication.
reviewNotes: Policies on MT and on generative AI are converging and change rapidly; guidance avoids naming specific tools.
Groves and Mundt (2015) is a proposed reference.

guidance.summary: Collaborative writing in L2 settings can support language learning through joint attention to form and meaning, although outcomes depend on how groups interact (Storch, 2011). Digital tools make collaboration visible and asynchronous but introduce new pragmatic demands: comments are a short written feedback genre in which tone and specificity matter (Hyland & Hyland, 2019). Lea and Jones (2011) caution against treating such practices as merely technical. Teaching should combine tool functions with comment-writing pragmatics and agreed group protocols.

activities.title: Comment pragmatics
learnerActions: Rank sample comments by usefulness and tone
Rewrite blunt or vague comments so that they are specific and appropriately mitigated
Practise replying to a critical comment
Agree a commenting protocol for their group
activities.intendedInsight: Comments are short, persistent texts whose tone affects collaboration.
activities.rationale: Treats comments as a feedback genre with its own pragmatics (Hyland & Hyland, 2019).

activities.title: Version history detective
learnerActions: Make and track changes in a shared document over a week
Use version history to identify who changed what
Restore a deleted section
Write a contribution statement based on the history
activities.intendedInsight: Version history is both a safety net and a record of contribution.
activities.rationale: Supports fair assessment of group work by giving learners evidence of their own contributions.

difficulties.pattern: Overwriting other people’s text directly.
difficulties.revealedBy: Disputes within groups; text lost without trace.
difficulties.response: Agree protocols at the outset, with suggestion mode as the default for others’ sections.

difficulties.pattern: Hesitating to comment on peers’ or supervisors’ text, or to reply to comments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Few or only positive comments; supervisor comments left unanswered.
difficulties.response: Model comments that are mitigated but specific, and treat polite, reasoned disagreement as expected.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to reply to a supervisor’s comment that they disagree with.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Writes a polite, reasoned reply that gives evidence and proposes a way forward.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accepts the change without engaging, or replies bluntly.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Ignores or deletes the comment.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: group projects in shared documents. UG and PGT in-sessional: group assessments and supervisor feedback on dissertations in shared files.

guidance.summary: File management is seldom taught but underpins all extended work. At doctoral level it becomes research data management, framed internationally by principles that data be findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable (Wilkinson et al., 2016) and included in researcher development frameworks under research management (Vitae, 2010). For taught students, simple naming conventions and tested backup routines are the priority.

activities.title: Naming convention design
learnerActions: Audit their current downloads or documents folder
Agree a naming convention as a class (e.g., date_module_task_version)
Rename and reorganise one module’s files
Explain the convention to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Consistent conventions make retrieval fast and prevent submitting the wrong version.
activities.rationale: Making the convention explicit and shared turns an individual habit into a checkable routine.

activities.title: Disaster drill
learnerActions: Imagine their device fails the day before a deadline and list what would be lost
Set up an off-device backup and test restoring a file
Write a one-paragraph plan for their files (research students: an outline data management plan)
Compare plans in pairs
activities.intendedInsight: A backup counts only if restoring from it works.
activities.rationale: Introduces research data management principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016) at a scale suited to the learner’s stage.

difficulties.pattern: final_FINAL_v3_really.docx
difficulties.revealedBy: Submitting the wrong version; inability to find earlier drafts.
difficulties.response: Introduce date-based version names or reliance on version history, and a single folder for submitted versions.

difficulties.pattern: “It’s in the cloud, so it’s backed up.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Synced deletions; a single cloud account as the only copy.
difficulties.response: Explain the difference between synchronisation and backup, and keep at least one independent copy.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show where the submitted version of their last assignment is and how they would recover it after device failure.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Shows a clear structure and version naming, and describes a backup they have tested.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Has some structure but an untested or single backup.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no system and a single copy.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and UG in-sessional: naming conventions and backups. PGT: dissertation files and project data. PGR: data management plans and ethics requirements for storing research data.
reviewNotes: Low language content; included for workflow and research-integrity reasons. A separate PGR topic on research data management may be warranted.
Wilkinson et al. (2016) is a proposed reference.

guidance.summary: Research on student emails to faculty (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007; Economidou-Kogetsidis, 2011) shows how pragmatic choices in digital messages, such as directness, mitigation and forms of address, shape how students are perceived, and that the relevant norms are rarely taught explicitly. The same principle extends to forums, chats and social media, where channel norms vary and messages persist. For research students, online presence becomes part of professional identity. Teaching should make channel norms explicit and open to discussion rather than prescriptive.

activities.title: Channel shift
learnerActions: Rewrite one message for three channels (group chat, course forum, professional networking site)
Compare choices of greeting, length, directness and emoji or abbreviation use
Discuss which choices peers find appropriate and why
Formulate channel norms for their own course
activities.intendedInsight: Appropriateness depends on channel and relationship, not on a single formal standard.
activities.rationale: Extends findings on email pragmatics (Economidou-Kogetsidis, 2011) to other digital channels.

activities.title: Online presence audit
learnerActions: Search for their own name online
Review what is visible to a prospective supervisor or employer
Decide what to change, remove or add
Research students: set up or update a researcher profile and identifier
activities.intendedInsight: Online presence is persistent and can be curated.
activities.rationale: Makes visible a dimension of academic identity that is often left tacit.

difficulties.pattern: Carrying peer-messaging norms into messages to staff.
difficulties.revealedBy: No greeting, heavy abbreviation, unmitigated demands in messages to tutors.
difficulties.response: Make channel norms explicit and explain their effect on readers. Avoid moralising or presenting one variety of politeness as universally correct.

difficulties.pattern: Sharing research or personal information too freely.
difficulties.revealedBy: Posting unpublished findings or potentially identifiable participant details.
difficulties.response: Connect online sharing to research ethics, confidentiality and data protection.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to draft a forum reply disagreeing with a classmate’s post.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Acknowledges the post, disagrees with reasons, mitigates appropriately and is concise.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Is polite but vague, or clear but blunt.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses an inappropriate tone or does not address the point.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: channel norms, forums and video calls. UG and PGT in-sessional: group chats and professional networking. PGR: researcher profiles, identifiers and public engagement online.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with prg.messaging-channels; this topic emphasises online presence, privacy and synchronous digital interaction.

guidance.summary: Stevenson’s (2016) critical interpretive synthesis of AWE in classrooms finds that the tools focus mainly on surface features, that their value depends heavily on how teachers integrate them, and that they work best as one source of feedback among several. Stevenson and Phakiti’s (2014) review found little evidence that gains from computer-generated feedback transfer to writing quality more generally. As generative AI is embedded in many editing tools, the boundary between feedback and rewriting is blurred, so awareness of what is permitted is part of this topic.

activities.title: Accept or reject, with reasons
learnerActions: Run their own paragraph through an AWE tool
Work through ten suggestions, accepting or rejecting each
Write a one-line reason for every decision
Compare decisions with a partner and resolve disagreements by checking a grammar reference or a corpus
activities.intendedInsight: Tools suggest; writers decide.
activities.rationale: Positions AWE as one input mediated by learner judgement, as Stevenson (2016) recommends.

activities.title: What the tool cannot see
learnerActions: Submit a paragraph that is grammatically clean but weakly argued to an AWE tool
Note how few issues are flagged
Peer-review the same paragraph for argument and evidence
Compare the two kinds of feedback
activities.intendedInsight: Surface correctness is not the same as quality.
activities.rationale: Illustrates the surface focus documented by Stevenson (2016) and the limited transfer reported by Stevenson and Phakiti (2014).

difficulties.pattern: Accepting every suggestion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Technical terms replaced, unidiomatic rephrasings, a flattened voice.
difficulties.response: Require a reason for every accepted change. Do not ban the tools; teach principled use.

difficulties.pattern: “If the checker finds no errors, the writing is good.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Content and structure left unrevised once surface errors are cleared.
difficulties.response: Separate global revision from surface editing in the drafting process and in feedback.

difficulties.pattern: Using rewriting or paraphrasing features that breach policy.
difficulties.revealedBy: Integrity concerns; submitted text that no longer reflects the learner’s own wording.
difficulties.response: Discuss institutional policy and distinguish feedback (diagnosis) from rewriting (production).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain why they rejected a particular suggestion from a checker.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a grounded reason (technical term, disciplinary convention, change of meaning).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a vague reason (‘it sounded wrong’).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no basis for the decision, or accepts all suggestions.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: critical use and policy awareness. UG and PGT in-sessional: integrating AWE output with feedback literacy, and awareness of generative-AI features in editing tools.
reviewNotes: AWE and generative-AI feedback are converging; evidence on newer AI-based feedback tools is still emerging.
Stevenson and Phakiti (2014) is a proposed reference.

guidance.summary: Kress and van Leeuwen (2006) propose a ‘grammar of visual design’ in which composition (information value, salience and framing) organises meaning much as grammar does in language; their Given–New and Ideal–Real zones are useful heuristics, though their cross-cultural generality is debated. Rowley-Jolivet’s (2002) study of conference presentations shows how much scientific argument is carried visually. The multiliteracies tradition (New London Group, 1996) argues that literacy education must include such design. Teaching should give learners a small, usable metalanguage and apply it to texts from their own disciplines.

activities.title: Eye path
learnerActions: View a poster for ten seconds and sketch the order in which they noticed its elements
Compare sketches in groups and identify shared paths
Relate the shared paths to design features (size, contrast, position, framing)
Redesign one element to change the path and test the new version on another group
activities.intendedInsight: Design creates reading paths; salience is engineered rather than accidental.
activities.rationale: Applies Kress and van Leeuwen’s (2006) concepts of salience and composition to a quick perceptual task.

activities.title: Image–text division of labour
learnerActions: Take a slide, or a figure with its caption, from their field
List what the image conveys and what the text conveys
Remove one mode and assess what is lost
Discuss differences between disciplines represented in the group
activities.intendedInsight: Modes are not redundant: each carries meaning the other does not.
activities.rationale: Builds on Rowley-Jolivet’s (2002) finding that visuals carry argument, not decoration, in scientific talks.

difficulties.pattern: “Visuals are decoration added after the writing is finished.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Clip art and stock images unrelated to content; visuals added at the last minute.
difficulties.response: Ask what each visual contributes to the argument and remove those that contribute nothing.

difficulties.pattern: Treating left-to-right reading-path heuristics as universal.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assuming Given–New left–right layout applies in every script and context.
difficulties.response: Present compositional zones as conventions associated with left-to-right writing systems and invite learners to compare layouts from their other languages.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain why the most important finding on a given poster is, or is not, in the right place.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses salience, position and framing concepts and links them to reader needs.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises that position matters but cannot explain the mechanism.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges by aesthetic preference only.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: basic awareness through posters and textbooks. Pre-sessional: analysis in preparation for poster and presentation assessments. UG and PGT in-sessional: discipline genres and professional visual communication.
reviewNotes: Kress and van Leeuwen’s compositional zones derive largely from Western media texts; their universality is contested.

guidance.summary: MacIntosh-Murray (2007) analyses the conference poster as a genre with its own forms, norms and values, noting the gap between advice that favours concise, visual posters and the text-heavy posters often produced in practice. Kress and van Leeuwen’s (2006) concepts of composition help learners design reading paths and salience deliberately. Because posters serve conversation in a session, design should anticipate the presenter’s spoken explanation, which is developed in the presentations strand.

activities.title: Poster gallery critique
learnerActions: Examine a set of real posters from a conference or departmental display
Rate each for clarity of main message at two metres, reading path and text density
Identify features shared by the most effective posters
Draft design principles for posters in their own discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Effective posters prioritise one message and are designed for viewing at a distance.
activities.rationale: Uses authentic exemplars to surface genre norms, in line with MacIntosh-Murray’s (2007) genre perspective.

activities.title: Word-budget redesign
learnerActions: Set a word budget for their own poster draft
Cut text to fit, converting prose results into captioned figures
Restructure the poster along a clear reading path
Test it with a peer who has 60 seconds to state the main message
activities.intendedInsight: A word budget forces prioritisation of claims.
activities.rationale: Applies salience and composition (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006) under a realistic constraint.

difficulties.pattern: Putting the essay or abstract on the poster.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dense paragraphs in small type; the full text of an abstract or introduction.
difficulties.response: Use word budgets and distance testing, and model how to cut. Simply saying ‘use less text’ rarely helps.

difficulties.pattern: Decoration before hierarchy.
difficulties.revealedBy: Background images, many colours and fonts, and no clear entry point.
difficulties.response: Establish the hierarchy (headline, key figure, supporting sections) first and add decoration last, if at all.

diagnostic.task: Show the learner’s poster draft to a peer, who has 30 seconds to identify the main finding.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The peer identifies the intended main finding correctly and quickly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The peer identifies the topic but not the main finding.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The peer cannot identify the topic or the finding.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: poster projects as assessed tasks. UG in-sessional: discipline posters, often produced in groups. PGT: dissertation posters. PGR: conference posters, whose norms vary by field and event.

guidance.summary: Visual summaries combine data visualisation with multimodal composition. Kress and van Leeuwen (2006) provide concepts for structuring visual hierarchy, while Tufte’s (2001) principles of graphical integrity guard against distortion. For public audiences, transparent number formats such as natural frequencies and absolute risks are generally clearer than relative ones (Gigerenzer et al., 2007). Teaching should balance impact with accuracy and stress the selection of a single message.

activities.title: Abstract to infographic
learnerActions: Identify the core finding and two supporting points in a research abstract
Sketch a layout on paper before using any software
Choose number formats suited to the audience
Ask a peer to check the sketch against the abstract for accuracy
activities.intendedInsight: Simplification requires selection without distortion.
activities.rationale: Combines composition (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006) with transparent number communication (Gigerenzer et al., 2007).

activities.title: Accuracy audit
learnerActions: Analyse a published infographic related to their field
Compare its claims with the study it summarises
Identify oversimplifications, distorted graphics or lost qualifications
Propose specific revisions
activities.intendedInsight: Visual summaries can overstate findings.
activities.rationale: Applies graphical integrity principles (Tufte, 2001) to a popular genre.

difficulties.pattern: “An infographic is about making it look attractive.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Icons and colour with no clear message or hierarchy.
difficulties.response: Plan the message first and the visuals second.

difficulties.pattern: Losing hedges in simplification.
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘X cures Y’ summarising ‘X was associated with modest improvement in Y’.
difficulties.response: Keep essential qualifications in plain language (linked to, in one study, for some patients).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state the core message and audience of an infographic they have drafted and point to how the design supports them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a single clear message, uses audience-appropriate numbers and keeps qualifications accurate.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a clear message, but the infographic contains inaccuracies or has lost qualifications.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no clear message, or misrepresents the source.

guidance.contextNotes: UG in-sessional: assessed infographics and public-facing tasks. PGT: professional audiences, especially in policy and health communication. PGR: visual abstracts for journals and public-engagement materials.

guidance.summary: The multiliteracies agenda (New London Group, 1996) argued that literacy education must address multimodal design, and Hafner (2014) describes language learners producing digital videos as ‘multimodal ensembles’ that combine semiotic resources for real audiences. Digital assessments keep the core academic requirements of argument, evidence and attribution, so the teaching challenge is to help learners see which conventions transfer and which change. Clear criteria and exemplars matter, because learners and staff may hold different expectations of these newer genres.

activities.title: Transfer analysis
learnerActions: Compare an essay brief and a video-essay brief on the same topic
List which criteria are shared and which are specific to the medium
Analyse an exemplar video essay for how argument and citation are realised
Draft a storyboard for their own topic
activities.intendedInsight: Academic criteria persist across media; their realisation changes with mode.
activities.rationale: Exemplar analysis supports genre awareness in newer digital genres such as those described by Hafner (2014).

activities.title: Mode orchestration storyboard
learnerActions: Plan a one-minute segment in columns for narration, on-screen text, image and sound
Check that each mode adds something the others do not
Identify the source of every media element and how it will be attributed
Review a partner’s storyboard for redundancy and clarity
activities.intendedInsight: Modes should complement rather than duplicate one another.
activities.rationale: Applies multimodal design thinking (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006) at the planning stage, where changes are cheapest.

difficulties.pattern: “It isn’t a real essay, so the academic rules don’t apply.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed images and music; opinion without evidence.
difficulties.response: Highlight the criteria shared with written assignments and model spoken and on-screen citation.

difficulties.pattern: Reading a written essay aloud over slides.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dense script in written register; monotone delivery.
difficulties.response: Script for the ear: shorter sentences, explicit signposting and rehearsal.

difficulties.pattern: Technical production dominates the work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Most time spent on editing software rather than content; anxiety about tools.
difficulties.response: Separate content planning from production and allow simple tools; assess the argument, not the effects.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they will cite a source in a podcast or video essay.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Plans spoken attribution plus a reference list in the required style (in show notes, credits or an accompanying document).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions the source orally but plans no formal reference.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Plans no attribution.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: short podcasts or recorded presentations, sometimes used in progression assessment. UG in-sessional: video essays and e-portfolios across many disciplines. PGT: professional portfolios and digital outputs.
reviewNotes: Two of the three key references for this topic (New London Group, 1996; Hafner, 2014) are proposed additions; if they are not accepted, Kress and van Leeuwen (2006) remains as support.

guidance.summary: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (World Wide Web Consortium, 2023) set out testable success criteria, such as text alternatives for non-text content, sufficient contrast and not relying on colour alone, which are widely applied to documents and teaching materials as well as web pages. The APA manual (American Psychological Association, 2020) also addresses accessible formatting. For EAP learners, accessibility is partly a language task: concise, informative alternative text and descriptive link text draw on summarising and data commentary. It is best taught as a design requirement from the outset.

activities.title: Alternative text for a chart
learnerActions: Write brief alternative text for a chart, stating its type and key message
Write a longer description for the same chart
Listen to both with a screen reader
Revise for concision and informativeness
activities.intendedInsight: Alternative text must convey the point of a visual, not merely its existence.
activities.rationale: Text alternatives are a core accessibility requirement (World Wide Web Consortium, 2023), and writing them practises selective summarising.

activities.title: Check and repair
learnerActions: Run an accessibility checker on one of their own assignments
Classify the issues flagged
Fix structural issues using styles
List issues the checker cannot detect, such as the quality of alternative text
activities.intendedInsight: Automated checks help, but they cannot judge meaning.
activities.rationale: Combines tool use with human judgement, mirroring how accessibility criteria are applied in practice.

difficulties.pattern: Formatting headings by making text bold and large.
difficulties.revealedBy: No heading structure visible in the navigation pane; screen readers cannot navigate.
difficulties.response: Teach styles and demonstrate screen-reader navigation of a structured and an unstructured version.

difficulties.pattern: Alternative text that says ‘image’ or repeats the caption.
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘Graph 1’, ‘picture’, or alternative text identical to the caption.
difficulties.response: Explain that a caption serves all readers while alternative text substitutes for the visual; write it for purpose.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write alternative text for a figure in their own work.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Conveys the type and key message concisely and offers a longer description where the figure is complex.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the type but not the message.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives generic alternative text or none.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: basic structure and alternative text in submitted work. UG and PGT in-sessional: slides, posters and dissertations. PGR: theses deposited in repositories, publications and teaching materials.
reviewNotes: Legal accessibility requirements vary by jurisdiction and institution and are not specified here.

guidance.summary: Quantity expressions draw on grammatical systems (quantifiers, partitives, number agreement and determiners) that corpus grammars describe in detail (Biber et al., 1999) and that pedagogical grammars identify as persistently difficult (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999). Learners usually control the mathematics; errors tend to lie in the English packaging. Teaching should focus on high-frequency academic patterns and on style-guide conventions for numerals (American Psychological Association, 2020), with oral practice to link spoken and written forms.

activities.title: Same quantity, four ways
learnerActions: Express a set of quantities as a decimal, a percentage, a fraction and a ‘one in n’ phrase
Choose the clearest form for a specified reader (specialist or general public)
Write each in a sentence with correct agreement
Check a partner’s sentences against a pattern sheet
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent quantities differ in clarity for different readers, and each form has its own grammar.
activities.rationale: Links form choice to audience, anticipating the argument that natural-frequency formats are often clearer for lay readers (Gigerenzer et al., 2007).

activities.title: Data-rich dictogloss
learnerActions: Listen to a short data-rich passage read aloud at natural speed
Note all the numbers and key words
Reconstruct the passage in writing in small groups
Compare with the original, focusing on quantity structures and agreement
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken and written number forms differ (‘nought point five’, ‘two point three million’), and both must be controlled.
activities.rationale: Collaborative reconstruction draws attention to form within meaningful content, and connects reception of spoken numbers with written accuracy.

difficulties.pattern: Using per cent and percentage interchangeably.
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘A high per cent of students’; ‘the percentage rose by 5 per cent’ when a five-point rise was meant.
difficulties.response: Teach the two as a contrast pair (per cent follows a number; percentage names a proportion) and return to the point when relative and absolute change are taught.

difficulties.pattern: Agreement after fractions and percentages (‘a third of the students was’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Singular verbs after plural of-complements, or plural verbs after uncountable ones.
difficulties.response: Teach agreement with the of-complement in partitives, using examples from learners’ own data. Avoid over-correcting notional agreement that is acceptable in expert usage.

difficulties.pattern: Decimal and digit-grouping marks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Writing 3,5 for three and a half or 1.000 for one thousand, leading to ambiguous figures.
difficulties.response: Where a learner’s other languages or schooling use the comma as the decimal marker and the point or space for thousands, make the convention explicit. The SI Brochure (BIPM, 2019) permits either decimal marker but recommends a space rather than a comma or point for grouping digits; English-language style guides generally use the decimal point, so follow the required guide consistently.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to correct five sentences containing quantity errors and explain each correction.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Corrects all five and states the rule involved (agreement with the of-complement, per cent versus percentage, decimal point).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Corrects most errors but cannot explain them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misses agreement and per cent/percentage errors.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: high priority, ideally coordinated with subject mathematics and science teaching. Pre-sessional: within data commentary and project writing. UG in-sessional: as a targeted focus where errors persist in reports.

guidance.summary: Approximators of quantity, degree and frequency are classed as hedges in taxonomies of scientific discourse (Salager-Meyer, 1994; Hyland, 1998), which shows that rounding and approximation are epistemic choices rather than stylistic ones. Channell’s (1994) work on vague language similarly shows that approximation is often communicatively appropriate rather than a failure of precision. Style guides such as the APA manual (American Psychological Association, 2020) advise reporting figures to a precision the measurement warrants. Teaching should pair approximation language with judgements about measurement precision and audience.

activities.title: Approximation accuracy check
learnerActions: Match expressions (just under half, roughly a third, well over twice) to values
Identify mismatches in sample sentences (e.g., ‘nearly half’ for 41%)
Discuss where acceptable ranges begin and end
Write approximate versions of a set of exact figures and have a partner check them
activities.intendedInsight: Approximators have conventional ranges, and readers check them against the figures.
activities.rationale: Treats approximators as accountable claims, consistent with their classification as hedges (Salager-Meyer, 1994).

activities.title: Precision for purpose
learnerActions: Compare how the same finding is reported in a research article and in a press release or lay summary
Note the rounding and approximation used in each
Rewrite a results paragraph for a lay reader and a lay paragraph for a results section
Explain the trade-offs in each version
activities.intendedInsight: Appropriate precision depends on audience and genre; false precision undermines credibility as much as vagueness does.
activities.rationale: Shows approximation as an epistemic and rhetorical choice, in line with its treatment as hedging in research writing (Hyland, 1998).

difficulties.pattern: “Exact numbers always look more academic.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Percentages to two or more decimal places from very small samples; spurious precision in lay summaries.
difficulties.response: Discuss measurement precision and sample size, and follow the required style guide on decimal places.

difficulties.pattern: Using approximators without a quantity to modify.
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘About many’, ‘approximately most of the participants’.
difficulties.response: Show that approximators need a numerical or quantitative anchor, and contrast them with vague fillers (a lot, things).

diagnostic.task: Give ‘n = 23; 9 agreed’ and ask for one sentence for a results section and one for a lay summary.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Results: nine of the 23 participants (39%); lay: about four in ten, or just under 40%.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Figures are correct but the approximator is mismatched, or the percentage is over-precise (39.13%).
diagnostic.gapResponse: The approximation is inaccurate or no figure is given.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: core approximators alongside number expressions. Pre-sessional: approximation in data commentary and presentations. UG and PGT in-sessional: conventions for reporting precision, and adapting figures for lay summaries and public engagement.

guidance.summary: Gal (2002) identifies knowledge of basic statistical concepts and terms as one component of statistical literacy, alongside context knowledge, critical skills and dispositions. Sub-technical words whose statistical sense differs from everyday use are a well-known trap, with ‘significant’ the clearest case. Teaching should anchor terms in learners’ own disciplinary readings and methods (Creswell & Creswell, 2018) and in reporting conventions such as those of the APA manual (American Psychological Association, 2020), rather than in decontextualised glossaries.

activities.title: Two senses sort
learnerActions: Collect sentences containing significant, random, error, bias and normal from academic and non-academic texts
Sort them by everyday or technical sense
Rewrite everyday uses that would be ambiguous in a quantitative report (e.g., using substantial or notable)
Create a personal glossary entry recording both senses with an example of each
activities.intendedInsight: Some everyday words become technical terms in research and cannot then be used loosely.
activities.rationale: Explicit contrast of senses addresses the sub-technical vocabulary problem at the point where it affects meaning in learners’ writing.

activities.title: Methods-section term hunt
learnerActions: Read the methods and results sections of an article in their field
List every statistical term and symbol
Explain each to a peer in plain English
Check the explanations against a research methods textbook
activities.intendedInsight: Statistical vocabulary is best learned in the context of real methods and results sections.
activities.rationale: Grounds terms in authentic disciplinary use, with Creswell and Creswell (2018) as an accessible reference for checking.

difficulties.pattern: “Significant means important.”
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘This is a significant finding’ with no test; ‘significantly increased’ for purely descriptive data.
difficulties.response: In quantitative reports, reserve significant for statistical significance or qualify it, and offer alternatives (substantial, notable, marked).

difficulties.pattern: Memorising definitions without being able to apply them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correct glossary definitions alongside misuse in writing, such as reporting a mean for heavily skewed income data.
difficulties.response: Use application tasks (which summary statistic suits these data, and why?) rather than testing definitions alone.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain in two sentences why a median might be reported instead of a mean for household income.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that skew or extreme values pull the mean and that the median better represents a typical case.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Defines both terms correctly but does not give the reason.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot distinguish the two terms.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: descriptive terms in business, science and social science modules. Pre-sessional: terms met in data commentary and source reading. UG and PGT in-sessional: terms in the methods and results of projects and dissertations, ideally coordinated with research methods teaching.
reviewNotes: EAP teachers may lack statistical training; collaboration with subject or mathematics-support staff is advisable for this topic.

guidance.summary: The American Statistical Association statement (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) sets out widely endorsed principles: p-values indicate how incompatible data are with a specified model; they do not measure the probability that a hypothesis is true or the size or importance of an effect; and conclusions should not rest on a threshold alone. EAP learners need not compute statistics, but they must read and report them without distortion, which is the interpretive and critical capacity at the centre of Gal’s (2002) account of statistical literacy. Teaching should use learners’ own disciplinary sources and attend to the language of reporting as much as to the concepts.

activities.title: Principles applied to misreadings
learnerActions: Read a plain-language summary of the ASA principles on p-values
Match each principle to an example misinterpretation from student or media texts
Rewrite each misinterpretation accurately
Discuss which misinterpretations appear in the literature of their own field
activities.intendedInsight: Common ways of phrasing statistical results can encode misconceptions.
activities.rationale: Uses the ASA statement (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) as an authoritative reference point for correcting misreadings.

activities.title: Significance versus size
learnerActions: Compare two studies: one with a large sample, a small effect and p < .001; one with a small sample, a large effect and p = .08
Decide which finding matters more for a stated practical decision, and why
Write a two-sentence report of each with appropriate hedging and the effect size
Review a partner’s reports for over-claiming
activities.intendedInsight: Statistical significance and practical importance answer different questions.
activities.rationale: Operationalises the distinction emphasised in the ASA statement (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) and in arguments for estimation-based reporting (Cumming, 2014).

difficulties.pattern: “p < .05 means the hypothesis is proven, or 95% likely to be true.”
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘This proves that …’; ‘there is a 95% chance that the theory is correct’.
difficulties.response: Correct the misconception directly using the ASA principles and model hedged reporting. Do not attempt to teach full inferential theory in an EAP class.

difficulties.pattern: “Not significant means there was no effect.”
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘The intervention had no effect (p = .07)’.
difficulties.response: Discuss sample size and confidence intervals, and offer accurate phrasing (no statistically significant difference was detected; the interval includes both small negative and moderate positive effects).

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding the statistical parts of sources altogether.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries of quantitative articles that skip the results; visible anxiety when statistics come up in discussion.
difficulties.response: Start from consumer-level questions, make it acceptable not to know the computations, and refer learners to mathematics-support services.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to paraphrase, for a literature review, a results sentence that reports an effect size, a confidence interval and a p-value.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Retains the direction, magnitude and uncertainty of the effect with appropriate hedging and no over-claiming.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Keeps the direction accurate but drops magnitude or uncertainty, or overstates the finding.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misinterprets the result or says that it proves the hypothesis.

guidance.contextNotes: UG in-sessional: reading quantitative sources in the social and health sciences. PGT: literature reviews and dissertations in which accurate reporting of others’ findings is assessed. PGR: reporting one’s own and others’ statistics to field standards, alongside research methods training.
reviewNotes: Statistical reporting reform (estimation, Bayesian approaches) is ongoing and conventions differ between fields; the guidance stays at the level of widely agreed misinterpretations.

guidance.summary: Gigerenzer et al. (2007) document how relative risk reductions presented without baselines mislead patients, journalists and doctors alike, and argue for transparent representations such as absolute risks and natural frequencies. Gal (2002) places critical interpretation of such figures at the heart of statistical literacy. For EAP learners the difficulty is both conceptual and linguistic: English distinguishes per cent from percentage points, and comparatives with numbers encode different arithmetic. Activities should alternate calculation, phrasing and judgement of framing.

activities.title: Framing the same result
learnerActions: Take a health or policy finding reported as a relative change
Calculate the absolute change and express it as natural frequencies, using the baseline
Write three versions of the finding (relative, absolute, natural frequency)
Ask peers how impressive each version sounds and discuss the differences
activities.intendedInsight: Relative framings inflate perceived effects when baselines are small.
activities.rationale: Reproduces in miniature the framing effects described by Gigerenzer et al. (2007).

activities.title: Points or per cent?
learnerActions: Sort sentences according to whether they report percentage-point or percentage change
Correct sentences that confuse the two
Find examples in news and academic texts in their field
Write a rule card with a worked example
activities.intendedInsight: Percentage points measure the difference between two percentages; per cent changes are relative to the starting value.
activities.rationale: Separating the linguistic distinction from the calculation helps learners see that an apparently small wording change alters the claim.

difficulties.pattern: “A rise from 10% to 15% is a 5% rise.”
difficulties.revealedBy: Percentage-point changes reported as percentage changes, or the reverse.
difficulties.response: Calculate first, then phrase; avoid teaching only the verbal rule.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting headline relative figures uncritically.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays citing ‘50% more likely’ without any baseline.
difficulties.response: Make ‘of what?’ a habitual question and connect it to source evaluation.

diagnostic.task: Ask whether ‘risk doubled’ is alarming when the baseline is 1 in 10,000.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Converts to 2 in 10,000, explains that the absolute change is small and names the framing effect.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says the baseline matters but miscalculates or phrases the point unclearly.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts ‘doubled’ as a large change without considering the baseline.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: news and policy texts used as sources. UG in-sessional: health, economics and social science sources. PGT: dissertations and reviews, especially in health and policy, where framing affects recommendations.

guidance.summary: The SI Brochure (BIPM, 2019) is the authoritative reference for unit names, symbols and their typographic conventions, while style guides such as the APA manual (American Psychological Association, 2020) and journal instructions add field-specific rules and occasionally differ, for example on spacing before the percent sign. Errors are usually conventional (case, spacing, plurals) rather than conceptual, but they are highly visible to subject markers. Teaching should be brief, reference-led and embedded in learners’ own lab or methods writing.

activities.title: Unit error hunt
learnerActions: Edit a methods text that contains unit errors
Check each correction against an SI summary sheet
Classify the errors (case, spacing, plural, prefix, compound unit)
Turn the classification into a personal checklist
activities.intendedInsight: Unit conventions are rule-governed and can be checked against an authority.
activities.rationale: Reference-led editing builds the habit of consulting an authoritative source (BIPM, 2019).

activities.title: Style guide versus SI
learnerActions: Compare SI conventions with their department’s or target journal’s style guide
Note any divergences (e.g., spacing before % or °C)
Decide which convention applies to their current assignment
Explain the decision to a peer
activities.intendedInsight: Local conventions may override general standards; internal consistency matters most.
activities.rationale: Shows learners that conventions have sources and scope, using the APA manual (American Psychological Association, 2020) as a contrasting authority.

difficulties.pattern: Writing Kg or kgs.
difficulties.revealedBy: Capitalised or pluralised unit symbols, or full stops after symbols.
difficulties.response: Explain that unit symbols are mathematical entities rather than abbreviations, so ordinary capitalisation and plural rules do not apply.

difficulties.pattern: Inconsistent units within one document.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mixing ml and mL, or g/L and mg/ml, across text and tables.
difficulties.response: Build a final consistency check into proofreading, using the search function.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write three measurements from their lab notes in a sentence.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All symbols, prefixes and spacing are correct and consistent.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Minor spacing or case errors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Pluralised or wrongly capitalised symbols, or missing units.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: science and engineering foundation programmes. Pre-sessional: discipline-specific streams for STEM-bound learners. UG in-sessional: lab reports, where unit errors are frequently penalised.
reviewNotes: The SI Brochure prescribes a space before % and °C, whereas several style guides omit the space before %; learners should follow the required guide consistently.

guidance.summary: Mathematical discourse combines language, symbolism and visual display, each doing distinct work (O’Halloran, 2005). Learners who are mathematically competent may still struggle to integrate symbolic expressions into English sentences, to define variables and to read notation aloud unambiguously. The SI Brochure (BIPM, 2019) and the APA manual (American Psychological Association, 2020) give conventions for quantity symbols and displayed equations, and disciplines add their own. Teaching should be discipline-specific and use learners’ own course texts.

activities.title: Equation as sentence
learnerActions: Examine textbook passages in which displayed equations form part of sentences
Identify the punctuation and the where-clauses that define terms
Rewrite a passage in which equations are dropped in without integration
Read the revised passage aloud
activities.intendedInsight: Displayed equations are grammatical constituents of the sentences around them.
activities.rationale: Makes explicit how symbolic and verbal resources interlock in mathematical discourse (O’Halloran, 2005).

activities.title: Notation read-aloud
learnerActions: In pairs, read aloud a list of expressions from their field
Compare readings with model versions
Note ambiguities, especially of grouping, and how speakers resolve them
Prepare a one-minute spoken explanation of a key formula for a peer
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken mathematics needs explicit conventions for grouping and order that written notation shows visually.
activities.rationale: Oral rehearsal prepares learners for tutorials, presentations and vivas, where formulae must be explained without the page.

difficulties.pattern: Leaving variables undefined.
difficulties.revealedBy: Equations in reports with unexplained symbols, reflecting school or examination contexts where the meaning was shared.
difficulties.response: Adopt the rule that every symbol is defined on first use and give learners a checklist.

difficulties.pattern: Ambiguous verbalisation of grouping.
difficulties.revealedBy: ‘x plus y squared’ used for (x + y)².
difficulties.response: Teach grouping phrases (the quantity x plus y, all squared; the square of the sum of x and y).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to introduce a given formula in a sentence and define its terms.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Integrates the formula grammatically, defines all variables and uses a conventional relational verb.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Defines the variables but the integration or punctuation is flawed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives no definitions or verbalises the formula incorrectly.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: mathematics and engineering foundation programmes. UG and PGT in-sessional: engineering, economics, physics and quantitative social science reports. PGR: thesis and article conventions, including field-specific notation.
reviewNotes: Conventions differ considerably across mathematics, physics, engineering and economics; subject-specialist input is advisable.

authorNotes: dat.describing-diagrams overlaps fun.describing-process and fun.describing-structure. I scoped it as verbalising visual representations (flowcharts, cycles, structural diagrams, maps and plans) and made it depend on both FUN topics; FUN topics should not link back to it.
